section: Company by Company — How Each Giant Runs Its Storage
title: Four questions that decode any company's storage stack
body: This chapter walks through one company at a time and looks at its whole storage stack, every layer from top to bottom. For each company it asks four questions. First, what did they build and what did they buy? Second, how big is it, using only numbers the company published, with the year? Third, how do they scale it and change it, including notable migrations? Fourth, what is their philosophy: build vs buy, cloud vs on-prem, and one standard system vs many specialised systems?
deeper:
Earlier chapters taught storage one layer at a time: distributed file systems in Chapter 2, object storage in Chapter 3, databases and storage engines in Chapter 5, caches in Chapter 6, and lakes, tiering and archival in Chapter 7. This chapter turns the book sideways. Instead of one layer across many companies, it looks at one company across all layers.

It deliberately does not re-teach internals. When a name like Colossus, Tectonic or Dynamo appears, the mechanics live in Chapters 2, 3 or 5. The goal here is the shape of each company's stack and the reasons behind that shape.

The four questions are a reusable lens. Build vs buy tells you where a company thinks its advantage lies. Published scale, always tied to a year, keeps comparisons honest. Migrations reveal how a company changes a live system without breaking it. And philosophy (standardize vs polyglot, cloud vs on-prem) explains why two companies with similar workloads end up with very different stacks. You can apply the same four questions to your own organisation's storage.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter insist on asking how each company changes and migrates its storage, not just what it runs?
quiz.a: Migrations show how a company evolves a live system safely, which reveals its real engineering philosophy and gives reusable templates, beyond a static snapshot of components.

section: Company by Company — How Each Giant Runs Its Storage
title: Why some companies get long sections and Apple gets a paragraph
body: Companies publish about their storage very unevenly, so this chapter's sections differ in length. Google and Meta publish research papers. AWS publishes product pages and re:Invent talks. Netflix, Uber and LinkedIn publish engineering blogs. Apple publishes almost nothing. The chapter's rule is simple: when a fact has not been published, it says so instead of guessing. That is why several companies have entries like "not published" for scale or compliance rather than an estimate.
deeper:
This accuracy rule shapes how you should read every section. A long Google or Meta section does not mean their stacks are more important; it means they wrote peer-reviewed papers (SOSP, OSDI, FAST, NSDI and so on) with detailed numbers. A short Apple section does not mean Apple's storage is simple; Apple simply does not publish much.

You will see the rule applied explicitly several times. Netflix publishes design detail more than total bytes, so the chapter gives no total for its warehouse or Cassandra fleet. Uber, Netflix and LinkedIn get no compliance design description because the sources used do not include one. Microsoft has not published a single current exabyte total for Azure Storage. In the big comparison table, cells say "not published" or "not covered".

The lesson for a practitioner: when you compare companies, or benchmark your own system against them, separate what is published from what is folklore. Numbers also differ in kind (objects, bytes, requests per second) and year, so an unlabelled figure passed around in a meeting is often misleading.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to conclude that a company with a short section has a simpler storage stack?
quiz.a: Section length reflects how much the company publishes, not stack complexity. Apple, for example, publishes almost nothing, so gaps mean unknown, not simple.

section: How to read the stack diagrams
title: The six layers every company diagram uses
body: Every company in this chapter gets one diagram with the same six layers, bottom to top. The hardware or distributed file system (DFS) layer turns thousands of disks and flash drives into one pool. The blob or object layer holds large, immutable, unstructured data like photos, videos and files. Databases hold small structured records with keys and indexes. Caches put memory or flash in front of databases to absorb reads. The lake or warehouse holds analytics data, usually columnar files. Archival keeps cold data for years at the lowest cost per byte.
deeper:
Using identical layers for every company makes the stacks directly comparable. You can put Google's Colossus next to Meta's Tectonic next to Azure's stream layer and see that they play the same role, even though the names and designs differ.

Each layer optimises for something different. The DFS layer is about pooling raw capacity and handling failures across huge fleets. The blob layer is about cheap, durable storage of big immutable objects. Databases are about fast lookups and updates of small records. Caches trade memory cost for lower read latency and less database load. The lake is about scanning large volumes of data efficiently, which is why columnar files dominate there. Archival is about cost per byte over years, accepting slow access.

Not every company fills every layer with its own system. Netflix and Pinterest put AWS at the bottom. LinkedIn's archival approach is not published. Apple's lower layers are not published at all. When you draw your own organisation's stack with these six layers, the empty or bought layers are as informative as the built ones.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter force every company into the same six-layer diagram?
quiz.a: Same layers make stacks comparable: you can see which systems play the same role (for example Colossus vs Tectonic) and which layers a company builds, buys or leaves unpublished.

section: How to read the stack diagrams
title: The recurring pattern: few shared foundations, many specialised tops
body: The pattern that repeats across nearly every giant: build a small number of shared foundations and put many specialised systems on top. The foundation, usually a distributed file system or storage-node layer, is where scale and cost live. It pools disks, handles durability and determines cost per byte. The specialised systems on top, such as key-value stores, SQL databases, caches and warehouses, are where product needs live. This split lets a company standardize where efficiency matters and diversify where features matter.
deeper:
Examples appear throughout the chapter. Google has Colossus underneath Bigtable, Spanner and BigQuery. Meta has Tectonic underneath blob storage and the data warehouse. Azure has the stream layer inside storage stamps underneath blobs, tables, queues and managed disks. AWS has S3's storage nodes (ShardStore) and EBS underneath many services.

Why does this split work? Cost at scale is dominated by hardware utilisation, durability overhead (replication or erasure coding) and operational effort. Those are best optimised once, in one system that a dedicated team tunes. Product teams, meanwhile, need very different interfaces: a graph cache, a global SQL database, a columnar warehouse. Forcing all of them onto one database would hurt the products; giving each its own disk fleet would waste hardware.

The key takeaways restate this: most giants build one shared storage foundation and many specialised systems on top. When you design storage for a large organisation, ask which layer should be one shared thing and which layers can safely be many.

quiz.q: In the foundation-plus-specialised-systems pattern, why put cost optimisation in the foundation rather than in each specialised system?
quiz.a: Hardware utilisation and durability overhead are best tuned once across a pooled fleet; per-system fleets strand resources, while product-specific features belong in the systems on top.

title: Google's stack: almost everything sits on Colossus
body: Google's storage stack is built almost entirely in-house. At the bottom, disks and flash sit in D file servers. Above them is Colossus, the cluster file system used since about 2010. On Colossus sit Bigtable (wide-column, 2006), Spanner (global SQL, 2012) and F1 (Ads SQL on Spanner). Caches are in-process and memory caches in front of Bigtable and Spanner. The blob layer is Google Cloud Storage plus internal blob stores. Analytics runs on Dremel/BigQuery with Capacitor columnar files. Archival uses colder media and an Archive storage class.
deeper:
The shape to notice is how many layers route back to Colossus. Google Cloud Storage, the public object store launched in 2010, runs on Colossus according to Google. Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus. BigQuery reads Capacitor columnar files from Colossus. Even Colossus's own metadata lives in Bigtable, which itself stores data on a smaller Colossus.

That recursion is the core of Google's design: one storage foundation per cluster serves nearly every workload, and the specialised systems above it differ in data model and consistency, not in how they store bytes on disk.

Compared with the other companies in this chapter, Google is the purest build company. AWS also builds, but sells what it builds. Meta builds and open-sources. Netflix buys infrastructure from AWS. Google builds nearly every layer and uses it internally and through Google Cloud.

The caches row is modest in Google's diagram: in-process and memory caches in front of Bigtable and Spanner, plus Memorystore in the comparison table. The heavy lifting on tiering happens inside Colossus itself, as a later card explains.

quiz.q: What makes Colossus the centre of Google's stack rather than just one component among many?
quiz.a: GCS, Spanner, BigQuery and even Colossus's own metadata (via Bigtable) all store bytes on Colossus, so one foundation per cluster serves nearly every workload.

title: GFS to Bigtable to Colossus: the lineage of Google's foundation
body: GFS, described at SOSP in 2003, was Google's first cluster file system: one master, 64 MB chunks and 3 replicas. Bigtable, presented at OSDI in 2006, is a sorted, sparse, wide-column map built on top of GFS and later Colossus. Colossus, in use since about 2010 and described publicly in 2021, is the GFS successor. Its key change: file system metadata lives in Bigtable, served by scalable "Curators", instead of in a single master's memory.
deeper:
The lineage explains why Colossus exists. GFS's single master held all metadata in RAM, which Chapter 2 covers as its breaking point: as files multiplied, one machine's memory and CPU capped the whole cluster. Colossus removed that ceiling by moving metadata into Bigtable, a system that was already horizontally sharded and trusted inside Google.

This creates a neat recursion. Colossus stores its metadata in Bigtable; Bigtable stores its data on a smaller Colossus. The recursion ends at a small, simple base that is easy to run.

The payoff is published: Google's 2021 post says Colossus clusters scale to exabytes and tens of thousands of machines, and metadata scales over 100x beyond the largest GFS clusters, precisely because metadata moved into Bigtable. Curators serve metadata out of Bigtable, so metadata capacity grows horizontally rather than by buying a bigger master.

Meta later repeated the same move with Tectonic storing metadata in ZippyDB.

quiz.q: What GFS limitation did Colossus fix by storing metadata in Bigtable?
quiz.a: GFS kept all metadata in one master's RAM, capping cluster size. Bigtable shards metadata horizontally, so Colossus metadata scales over 100x beyond the largest GFS clusters.

title: Megastore, Spanner and F1: Google's SQL climb
body: Google built several database layers on its foundation. Megastore (CIDR 2011) grouped data into entity groups replicated with Paxos across data centers, on top of Bigtable. Spanner (OSDI 2012) is globally distributed SQL with external consistency, made possible by TrueTime, Google's clock-uncertainty API. F1 (VLDB 2013) is distributed SQL for the Ads business, built on Spanner. F1 existed so Ads could leave a manually sharded MySQL setup that was hard to reshard.
deeper:
The progression shows Google moving up the consistency and query-power ladder while keeping the same storage foundation. Bigtable gave scalable sorted key-value storage but no multi-row transactions across the dataset. Megastore added cross-data-center replication with Paxos, but only within entity groups. Spanner went further: SQL with externally consistent transactions across the globe, using TrueTime to bound clock uncertainty.

F1 is the application-facing proof. Google's Ads business, one of its most important revenue systems, ran on manually sharded MySQL. Resharding such a setup is painful: every time data outgrows a shard, engineers must split data and update routing by hand. F1 on Spanner replaced that with a database that handles sharding itself.

This is also a migration story. The chapter notes that Spanner replaced sharded MySQL for Ads, which is one of Google's two headline storage migrations alongside GFS to Colossus.

Throughout, Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus, so even a global SQL database is just another tenant of the shared file system foundation.

quiz.q: Why did Google build F1 on Spanner for the Ads business?
quiz.a: Ads ran on manually sharded MySQL that was hard to reshard. F1 on Spanner gave distributed SQL that handles sharding itself, removing manual resharding work.

title: Dremel, BigQuery and Cloud Storage: Google's analytics and blobs
body: Dremel, published at VLDB in 2010 and offered publicly as BigQuery from 2011, is a columnar, tree-structured query engine over nested data. It reads Capacitor columnar files stored on Colossus. Google Cloud Storage, launched in 2010, is Google's public object store, and Google says it runs on Colossus. Together they fill the lake/warehouse and blob layers of Google's stack, and both depend on the same file system foundation as Bigtable and Spanner.
deeper:
Dremel's tree structure lets one query fan out across many servers that each scan a slice of the data, with results combined on the way back. Storing data in columns means a query that touches three fields out of hundreds reads only those three, which is why columnar files dominate analytics everywhere (Chapter 7).

Capacitor is Google's columnar file format, and BigQuery reads it from Colossus. That means Google did not build a separate analytics storage cluster; analytics is simply another workload on the shared foundation.

Google Cloud Storage follows the same logic. In 2025 Google described a "Rapid Storage" zonal bucket type built directly on Colossus's stateful protocol. It supports 20 million requests per second in a single bucket with sub-millisecond latency. That number is notable because it shows a public object store exposing performance that comes straight from the internal file system.

For archival, Google uses colder media and an Archive storage class, again as tiers rather than a separate world.

quiz.q: What does Rapid Storage (2025) show about the relationship between Google Cloud Storage and Colossus?
quiz.a: It is built directly on Colossus's stateful protocol, so the public object store exposes internal file-system performance: 20 million requests per second per bucket, sub-millisecond latency.

title: Google's published scale: exabytes and 100x metadata
body: Google publishes few raw storage totals. What it has said: Colossus clusters scale to exabytes and tens of thousands of machines, and metadata scales over 100x beyond the largest GFS clusters because metadata moved into Bigtable (2021). In 2025 Google said the Rapid Storage zonal bucket type, built directly on Colossus's stateful protocol, supports 20 million requests per second in a single bucket with sub-millisecond latency. Both numbers describe capability limits, not total bytes stored.
deeper:
Notice what kind of numbers these are. Google does not say "we store N exabytes in total". It says a single cluster can reach exabytes, and metadata can scale over 100x beyond GFS. The Rapid Storage figure is a per-bucket request rate, not a fleet-wide one.

This matters when you line Google up against others. The chapter's side-by-side table lists Google Colossus as "exabyte clusters, 100x GFS metadata scale" (2021) and Google Rapid Storage as "20M requests per second in one bucket" (2025). Compare that with AWS S3's "700+ trillion objects, 200M+ requests per second average, hundreds of EB" (2026), which is a fleet-wide figure. These are different units and different scopes, so ranking them is meaningless.

The 100x metadata claim is the most telling engineering number. It quantifies what moving metadata out of a single master into a sharded database bought Google. It is the published evidence behind the senior staff lesson: put your metadata in a database you already trust.

The key takeaway at the end of the chapter warns exactly about this: published numbers differ in kind and year.

quiz.q: Why can't you directly rank Google's Rapid Storage figure against S3's 200M+ requests per second?
quiz.a: Rapid Storage's 20M is per single bucket (2025); S3's figure is a fleet-wide average (2026). Different scope, unit and year make a direct ranking meaningless.

title: Google's philosophy: layer everything on one foundation
body: Google is the purest build company: almost every storage layer is in-house. The key idea is layering on one foundation. GFS and then Colossus store the bytes. Bigtable stores Colossus's own metadata. Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus. BigQuery reads columnar files from Colossus. One storage foundation per cluster serves nearly every workload, so improvements to Colossus, such as better tiering or encoding, benefit every system above it at once.
deeper:
The chapter labels this a standardize philosophy at the bottom and a polyglot philosophy at the top. There are many databases (Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore, Memorystore), but they share one distributed file system. Teams get the data model they need without each running its own disk fleet.

The chapter also notes this is the same move Meta made with Tectonic roughly ten years later. Google got to a single foundation early; Meta first specialised (Haystack, f4, HDFS) and then consolidated.

Why does this pay off? When there is one foundation, capacity is pooled, so hot and cold workloads share disks and neither strands resources. Durability techniques like erasure coding are implemented once in the client library. Operational expertise concentrates in one team. And migrations get easier: when Google moved from GFS to Colossus, applications moved by changing libraries, not by rewriting, because the client library API stayed.

The risk is concentration: a bug in the foundation touches everything. Google mitigates by keeping the recursion's base small and simple.

quiz.q: What does 'standardize at the bottom, polyglot at the top' mean in Google's case?
quiz.a: Many databases (Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore, Memorystore) serve different product needs, but all share one distributed file system, Colossus, for storing bytes.

title: Senior staff lens: put metadata in a database you already trust
body: Google's big lesson is "put the metadata in a database you already trust". GFS broke because one master held all metadata in RAM. Colossus fixed that by storing metadata in Bigtable, which itself stores data on a smaller Colossus. The recursion ends at a small, simple base. When your own metadata service becomes the bottleneck, the question to ask is: can I store it in a sharded system I already operate, instead of building a bigger single master?
deeper:
The instinct when a metadata server runs out of memory is to buy a bigger machine or hand-shard it. Both hit limits: machines stop growing, and hand-sharded metadata is fragile. Google's move was to reuse a sharded, battle-tested database, so metadata scaling inherits that database's horizontal scaling, replication and operational tooling.

Meta reached the same answer independently. Tectonic splits metadata into Name, File and Block layers, each hash-partitioned and stored in ZippyDB, a Paxos key-value store on RocksDB. The chapter's key takeaways call this out: metadata scaling drove the biggest redesigns (GFS to Colossus, HDFS to Tectonic), and both moved metadata into a sharded key-value store.

LinkedIn shows the contrast. Its 2021 post describes a lot of work to keep a single HDFS NameNode healthy at very large object counts, which is the Chapter 2 metadata bottleneck in real life.

A caveat: the recursion must terminate. Colossus-on-Bigtable-on-Colossus works because the inner Colossus is small and simple enough not to need the same trick.

quiz.q: What is the common idea behind Colossus storing metadata in Bigtable and Tectonic storing metadata in ZippyDB?
quiz.a: Both move file-system metadata out of one master's memory into a horizontally sharded key-value store, so metadata capacity scales with the number of shards.

title: Colossus tiers by temperature so users don't have to
body: Google's 2021 Colossus post says new, hot data goes to flash and is spread evenly over all disks, and colder data moves to larger, cheaper drives as it ages. This is tiering by temperature, the idea from Chapter 7, but done inside the file system itself rather than by users choosing storage classes. Alongside this, Google scales metadata horizontally with Curators over Bigtable instead of making one master bigger. Both techniques keep scaling automatic and invisible to applications.
deeper:
Tiering by temperature exploits a near-universal access pattern: data is read most right after it is written and less over time. Putting fresh data on flash serves the heavy early reads quickly. Spreading it evenly over all disks avoids hotspots where a few drives absorb all new writes. As data cools, moving it to larger, cheaper drives lowers cost per byte without users noticing.

The important design choice is where tiering lives. Many systems push it to users: pick a storage class, write lifecycle rules, move data yourself. Google made it a file-system responsibility, so every system above Colossus (Bigtable, Spanner, BigQuery, Cloud Storage) gets tiering for free.

The "what to steal" list repeats this: tier by temperature inside the storage system so users do not have to.

The metadata side follows the same principle of scaling out, not up. Curators serve metadata backed by Bigtable, so adding capacity means adding Curators and Bigtable shards. Combined, these choices let one Colossus cluster reach exabytes and tens of thousands of machines.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of Google doing temperature tiering inside Colossus rather than asking users to manage storage classes?
quiz.a: Every system on Colossus gets tiering automatically; users need no lifecycle rules or manual moves, and hot data spreads evenly on flash while cold data shifts to cheaper drives.

title: Colossus lets each app choose durability via the client library
body: In Colossus, the client library does software RAID and erasure coding. That means encoding happens on the client side, not in a fixed server-side policy, so each application picks its own mix of durability and performance. One file system can then serve a latency-sensitive database and a cost-sensitive archive, each with a different recipe. The same client library API also made migration from GFS to Colossus possible by swapping libraries instead of rewriting applications.
deeper:
Client-side encoding is a quiet but powerful design choice. Replication (several full copies) gives fast reads and simple repair but costs more space. Erasure coding cuts storage overhead but makes writes and repairs more expensive. A single fixed policy would force every workload into one trade-off. Letting the client choose means each workload sits where it wants on that curve.

Meta's Tectonic uses the same idea, which the chapter calls tenant-specific client logic: blob storage writes replicated first and re-encodes to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed, while the warehouse uses RS(9,6) for long-lived data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle data.

The client library is also Google's migration lever. The chapter notes Google has not published a detailed GFS-to-Colossus migration story, but the design tells you how it worked: the new system kept a client library API, so applications moved by changing libraries rather than rewriting code. A stable client interface is what turns a file system replacement into a library upgrade.

quiz.q: How did keeping a client library API help Google migrate from GFS to Colossus?
quiz.a: Applications talked to storage through the library, so moving to Colossus meant swapping the library, not rewriting application code.

title: Google Cloud encrypts everything at rest by default
body: Google Cloud says all customer data is encrypted at rest by default, with no action needed by the customer. Customers who want more control can add their own keys, called customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). For data residency, Google offers region choice plus controls such as Assured Workloads, which constrain where data and workloads live. Chapter 11 covers the mechanics of encryption keys and residency controls in detail.
deeper:
Default-on encryption means there is no unencrypted mode for customers to forget to switch on. CMEK adds a layer: the customer controls the key, typically through a key management service, so revoking or rotating the key controls access to the data even though Google runs the storage.

Residency works through geography. Choosing a region pins where data is stored, and tools like Assured Workloads add guardrails so data and workloads stay within required boundaries.

This posture is now common across the big clouds, which the chapter's key takeaways emphasise: encryption at rest is a default, not an option, at AWS S3 (since 2023), Azure Storage and Google Cloud. The three differ in details. S3 encrypts all new objects by default with S3-managed keys and lets customers choose KMS keys. Azure encrypts with 256-bit AES by default and it cannot be turned off, with bring-your-own-key available.

The compliance posture sections are labelled "as published" because they report only what each company has documented publicly.

quiz.q: What does CMEK add on top of Google Cloud's default encryption at rest?
quiz.a: The customer controls the encryption key, so key rotation or revocation governs access to data, rather than relying only on Google-managed keys.

title: Amazon is both a storage customer and a storage seller
body: Amazon is two things at once: a retailer that uses storage and a cloud (AWS) that sells storage. The retail side famously wrote the Dynamo paper. The cloud side runs S3, EBS, DynamoDB, Aurora and many more. Its stack: AWS-designed servers, Nitro cards and HDD and SSD fleets at the bottom; S3 storage nodes running ShardStore; EBS network block volumes; DynamoDB and Aurora databases; ElastiCache and MemoryDB caches; a lake of S3 plus Athena, EMR, Redshift and S3 Tables; and S3 Glacier classes for archival.
deeper:
The dual identity shapes everything. Because AWS sells storage, it must build it: storage is literally its product, the first of the chapter's three axes. Because Amazon retail is expected to use what AWS sells, the retailer is also one of AWS's most demanding customers, which the chapter describes as a very strong form of "eat your own cooking".

In the comparison table, AWS's foundation column reads "ShardStore nodes, EBS", its object layer is S3, main online databases are DynamoDB and Aurora, caches are ElastiCache and MemoryDB, the lake is S3 plus Athena, Redshift and S3 Tables, archival is Glacier classes, cloud vs on-prem is "is the cloud", and build vs buy is "build, and retail uses AWS".

Hardware is custom too: AWS-designed servers and Nitro cards. This matters because the foundation layer, where cost and scale live, is fully under AWS's control, the same way Colossus is under Google's.

Unlike Google's single-foundation story, AWS exposes many separate services to customers, which the philosophy card explains as deliberate polyglot design.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say AWS must build its storage rather than buy it?
quiz.a: AWS sells storage: it is AWS's product. A company whose product is storage cannot outsource the thing it sells, and its retail side also consumes it.

title: Dynamo (2007) and DynamoDB (2012) are not the same design
body: Dynamo, described at SOSP in 2007, was Amazon's internal leaderless key-value store for the shopping cart. It used consistent hashing, sloppy quorums and vector clocks to stay available during failures. DynamoDB, launched in 2012, is AWS's managed key-value and document database. Despite the shared name, DynamoDB is not the same design as the 2007 Dynamo paper. Confusing the two is common: the paper describes an internal retail system, while DynamoDB is a separate managed service built later.
deeper:
The Dynamo paper became famous because it popularised leaderless replication for high availability: any replica could accept writes, conflicting versions were tracked with vector clocks, and sloppy quorums let writes proceed even when some preferred nodes were unreachable. LinkedIn's early Voldemort, for example, was a Dynamo-style key-value store.

DynamoDB's own paper, presented at USENIX ATC in 2022, describes a different set of priorities. Its team chose predictable performance over peak performance as the main goal, and most design choices, such as admission control, partition splitting and global admission control, serve that goal.

The scale DynamoDB now handles is published: on Prime Day 2024 it served tens of trillions of calls with a peak of 146 million requests per second.

Practical pitfall: if you reason about DynamoDB's consistency or conflict behaviour from the 2007 paper, you will get it wrong. Always check which system a design claim refers to. The chapter explicitly flags that the two are not the same design.

quiz.q: Why is it a mistake to reason about DynamoDB's behaviour using the 2007 Dynamo paper?
quiz.a: DynamoDB (2012) is a different design from the internal 2007 Dynamo; its priorities, like predictable performance via admission control, differ from Dynamo's leaderless, vector-clock approach.

title: S3, EBS, Glacier and Express One Zone: AWS's byte stores
body: AWS's main byte stores span the stack. S3, launched in 2006, is the object store; it has offered strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020. EBS, from 2008, provides network block storage volumes for EC2 virtual machines (Chapter 4). Glacier, from 2012, was archival storage and now exists as S3 storage classes. S3 Express One Zone, from 2023, is a single-zone, low-latency S3 class for hot data. Together they cover hot, block, general object and cold storage.
deeper:
Each service targets a different point on the cost and latency curve. EBS gives virtual machines disks over the network, which is what databases and file systems on EC2 need. S3 is the general-purpose object store behind lakes, backups and application data. Glacier classes trade retrieval speed for the lowest cost per byte. Express One Zone moves the other direction: by keeping data in a single availability zone, it lowers latency for hot data, accepting less geographic redundancy.

Glacier's evolution from a separate service into S3 storage classes mirrors Google's approach of tiering within one system: customers stay in one namespace and move data between classes.

Scale is published for both. S3's page in 2026 shows more than 700 trillion objects and more than 200 million requests per second on average. For Prime Day 2024, Amazon provisioned 264 PB of EBS and performed 5.6 trillion EBS I/Os.

The S3 consistency change in 2020 is a headline migration in its own right, covered in a later card as the model for upgrading a contract in place.

quiz.q: What trade-off does S3 Express One Zone make compared with standard S3?
quiz.a: It keeps data in a single availability zone to give lower latency for hot data, giving up the multi-zone redundancy of standard S3 classes.

title: Aurora: the log is the database
body: Aurora, launched in 2014 with a paper in 2017, is AWS's relational database built on log-structured shared storage. Its core idea is "the log is the database": only redo log records cross the network, sent to a storage layer that keeps six replicas. The storage layer applies the log to build data pages itself. This cuts network traffic compared with shipping full data pages, and it separates database compute from a shared, replicated storage service.
deeper:
In a traditional relational database, the engine writes both log records and full data pages to disk, and replication sends even more data across the network. Aurora sends only redo log records, which are small descriptions of changes. The storage layer, replicated six ways, materialises pages from the log. Less data on the network means higher write throughput.

Six-way replication gives durability and availability even when replicas fail, and because storage is a shared service rather than attached to one server, compute nodes can be replaced or added without copying the whole database.

Microsoft reached a similar idea with Socrates (SQL Hyperscale, 2019), which splits SQL Server into compute, a log service and page servers over Azure Storage. The shared lesson is that splitting compute from storage lets each scale independently.

Aurora's scale on Prime Day 2024: 6,311 instances processed 376 billion transactions. Aurora was also one of the destinations when Amazon's consumer business migrated off Oracle in 2019, alongside DynamoDB and Redshift.

quiz.q: Why does sending only redo log records to storage help Aurora's throughput?
quiz.a: Log records are much smaller than full data pages, so far less data crosses the network; the six-way replicated storage layer rebuilds pages itself.

title: ShardStore: a Rust storage node checked with formal methods
body: ShardStore, described at SOSP in 2021, is the Rust key-value storage node software running inside S3's storage nodes. It replaced earlier storage node software behind the same S3 API, so customers saw no change. AWS validated ShardStore with lightweight formal methods: property-based testing and model checking against a simple reference model. This is how AWS changes low-level storage code safely at exabyte scale, where a subtle bug could corrupt enormous amounts of data.
deeper:
A reference model is a deliberately simple implementation of the expected behaviour, for example a plain in-memory map. Property-based testing generates huge numbers of random operation sequences, runs them against both ShardStore and the model, and checks that results match. Model checking explores interleavings and failure scenarios systematically. Together they catch bugs that ordinary unit tests miss, such as corner cases in crash recovery.

Why "lightweight"? Full formal verification of a production storage engine is extremely expensive. Checking against a reference model gives much of the confidence at a fraction of the cost, and it runs continuously as engineers change code.

The ShardStore swap is a migration pattern the chapter highlights twice: new storage node software replaced old software inside S3, behind the same API. Along with S3's move to strong consistency, it shows AWS evolving the internals of a massive service without asking customers to do anything.

The "what to steal" list turns this into advice: use formal methods and reference models for storage node code.

quiz.q: What role does the simple reference model play in validating ShardStore?
quiz.a: It defines expected behaviour; randomized tests and model checking compare ShardStore's results against it, catching subtle bugs such as crash-recovery corner cases.

title: S3's published scale: 700 trillion objects, hundreds of exabytes
body: As shown on the AWS S3 page in 2026, S3 stores more than 700 trillion objects, serves more than 200 million requests per second on average, and holds "hundreds of exabytes". These are fleet-wide figures across the whole service. They make S3 the largest published storage system in this chapter by object count, and they explain why AWS cares so much about spreading load, isolating failures and changing node software safely.
deeper:
The request figure is an average, not a peak, which is worth pausing on: at 200 million requests per second on average, even a small percentage of hot objects or noisy customers could overwhelm individual disks if data were not spread carefully.

That is where S3's heat management comes in. Objects are spread over very many disks so no single disk sees too much traffic. AWS has described this in re:Invent talks, and the principle is that at huge scale the aggregate load becomes smooth even when each customer is spiky. Scale, in other words, is not only a challenge but also a tool: more customers make the total more predictable.

The side-by-side scale table lists AWS S3 as "700+ trillion objects, 200M+ requests per second average, hundreds of EB" (2026). Compare carefully: Meta's Tectonic figure of 1,590 PB is one cluster's capacity in 2021, and Google's Rapid Storage figure is per bucket in 2025. Units, scope and year all differ.

quiz.q: How does S3's enormous scale actually make load easier to manage?
quiz.a: Spreading objects over very many disks means many spiky customers add up to a smooth aggregate load, so no single disk sees too much traffic.

title: Prime Day 2024 in numbers
body: AWS published Prime Day 2024 storage figures. DynamoDB served tens of trillions of calls with a peak of 146 million requests per second. ElastiCache served over a quadrillion requests in a day, peaking above 1 trillion requests per minute. Amazon provisioned 264 PB of EBS and performed 5.6 trillion EBS I/Os. Aurora ran 6,311 instances that processed 376 billion transactions. Prime Day is Amazon retail's biggest event, and it runs on AWS's own services.
deeper:
These numbers illustrate the "eat your own cooking" philosophy in practice. Amazon retail's peak shopping event is a stress test of AWS's databases, caches and block storage, not of some separate internal stack.

Look at the cache figure relative to the database figure. ElastiCache peaked above 1 trillion requests per minute, which is over 16 billion per second, far more than DynamoDB's 146 million per second peak. That ratio shows the role of caches from Chapter 6: they absorb the overwhelming majority of reads so databases see a manageable load.

EBS figures show that plenty of workloads still run on block storage attached to EC2 instances: 264 PB provisioned and 5.6 trillion I/Os.

Aurora's 6,311 instances show relational databases remain central even at a company famous for key-value stores.

When comparing, keep the unit in mind: DynamoDB's number is a peak per second, ElastiCache's peak is per minute, and EBS's is capacity provisioned. The chapter's side-by-side table lists DynamoDB's 146M peak and EBS's 264 PB, both for 2024.

quiz.q: What does the gap between ElastiCache's and DynamoDB's Prime Day 2024 peaks illustrate?
quiz.a: Caches absorb most reads: ElastiCache peaked above 1 trillion requests per minute versus DynamoDB's 146 million per second, keeping database load manageable.

title: Amazon's 2019 Oracle exit: 75 PB off 7,500 databases
body: In 2019 Amazon's consumer business finished migrating 75 PB of data from about 7,500 Oracle databases to AWS services such as DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift. The retailer moved off a bought database onto its own cloud's databases. The team used AWS Database Migration Service and rewrote many schemas to fit key-value models. The chapter calls this the proof of Amazon's philosophy: AWS builds what it sells, and Amazon retail is expected to use it.
deeper:
This migration was not a simple lift-and-shift. Moving from Oracle, a relational database, to DynamoDB, a key-value and document store, often requires redesigning data models: joins and ad hoc queries give way to access patterns designed around keys. That is why many schemas were rewritten, not just copied.

The destinations reflect AWS's polyglot stance. Workloads that fit key-value access went to DynamoDB. Relational workloads went to Aurora. Analytics went to Redshift. Each got a purpose-built system rather than one replacement for all of Oracle.

AWS Database Migration Service handled moving the data itself, letting teams focus on application and schema changes.

The strategic point is credibility. A cloud that tells customers to trust its databases is more convincing when its own retail business, at 75 PB scale, runs on them. It also removed the cost and dependency of a bought commercial database.

This fits the chapter's broader pattern of large migrations being deliberate and gradual, alongside Meta's MyRocks move, Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit.

quiz.q: Why did Amazon's Oracle exit involve rewriting many schemas instead of copying them?
quiz.a: Much data moved from relational Oracle to key-value DynamoDB, which needs data models designed around keys and access patterns rather than joins and ad hoc queries.

title: AWS philosophy: eat your own cooking, and polyglot on purpose
body: AWS builds everything it sells, and Amazon retail is expected to use what AWS sells, a very strong form of "eat your own cooking". AWS is also polyglot on purpose: it sells many purpose-built databases for key-value, relational, document, graph, time series and ledger workloads. The official line is "use the right tool for the job". The trade-off is that customers must pick well, which is why the book's Chapter 14 exists.
deeper:
Contrast this with Google's philosophy. Google also has many databases, but it stresses one foundation per cluster underneath. AWS's public face is a menu of distinct services, each with its own API, limits and pricing. Internally there are shared foundations too (S3's storage nodes, EBS), but customers experience AWS as many choices.

The strength of polyglot is fit: a graph workload on a graph database, a ledger on a ledger database, key-value on DynamoDB, relational on Aurora. Each can be optimised for its access pattern.

The weakness is decision burden and sprawl. A team can pick the wrong database, or an organisation can end up running a dozen databases with a dozen operational playbooks. The chapter's third axis addresses this: when hundreds of teams use storage, a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off choices; when only a handful do, polyglot by team is fine.

Eating its own cooking also keeps AWS honest: retail feels any weakness in AWS services before or alongside external customers.

quiz.q: What is the main downside of AWS's 'use the right tool for the job' polyglot approach?
quiz.a: Customers must choose correctly among many purpose-built databases; a wrong pick or too many different systems creates poor fit and operational sprawl.

title: DynamoDB picked one goal: predictable performance over peak
body: In industry: the DynamoDB paper, presented at USENIX ATC in 2022, says the team chose predictable performance over peak performance as its main goal. Most of DynamoDB's design choices serve that single goal, including admission control, partition splitting and global admission control. The chapter's advice: when you design a shared storage service, choose one primary goal like this and write it down, so every later design decision can be judged against it.
deeper:
Why predictability instead of speed? For a multi-tenant service, customers care more about consistent latency than about occasional record-breaking throughput. A database that is usually fast but sometimes stalls forces applications to add retries, timeouts and over-provisioning.

Each mechanism named in the paper supports predictability. Admission control limits how much work a partition accepts, so one tenant cannot overload shared resources. Partition splitting divides hot or growing partitions so load spreads. Global admission control coordinates limits across the fleet rather than per node.

The broader lesson is about decision-making in design. Shared storage services face endless trade-offs: latency vs throughput, cost vs durability, features vs simplicity. Without a written primary goal, each decision is argued from scratch and the system drifts. With one, the answer to "should we add this optimisation that raises peak throughput but adds jitter?" is obvious.

This is the first item under "what to steal from AWS": choose one primary goal for a shared service and derive every design choice from it. Prime Day 2024 shows it at scale: 146 million requests per second peak.

quiz.q: Why would a shared database prioritise predictable performance over peak performance?
quiz.a: Tenants need consistent latency; unpredictable stalls force retries and over-provisioning. Admission control and partition splitting keep one tenant or hotspot from disrupting others.

title: Cells and heat management: how AWS limits blast radius
body: AWS scales by splitting services into cells, independent slices of infrastructure, so one failure hits a slice of customers, not all of them (Chapter 10). Within S3, heat management spreads objects over very many disks so no single disk sees too much traffic. AWS has described this in re:Invent talks. The principle: at huge scale the aggregate load becomes smooth even when each customer is spiky. Together, cells contain failures and wide spreading contains hotspots.
deeper:
Cells are about blast radius. If a bad deployment, a software bug or a hardware fault hits one cell, only the customers in that cell are affected. Engineers can also roll out changes cell by cell, watching for problems before continuing. Azure's storage stamps are a related idea: fixed-size units that limit how much fails together.

Heat management is about hotspots. Any single customer's traffic is bursty: a viral file, a batch job, a traffic spike. If that customer's data sat on a few disks, those disks would overload while others idled. Spreading each customer's objects across very many disks means every disk carries a small share of many customers' traffic, and the random spikes average out. This is the statistical benefit of scale: the more independent workloads you pool, the steadier the total.

The two ideas complement each other. Cells answer "how much can fail together?" and heat spreading answers "how do we stop one customer's burst from melting a disk?". Both rely on scale: the more customers and disks there are, the smaller each slice and the smoother the total.

quiz.q: Why does spreading each customer's objects across many disks smooth load in S3?
quiz.a: Each disk then carries small slices of many customers' traffic, so independent spikes average out and no single disk is overwhelmed by one customer's burst.

title: S3's 2020 strong consistency: upgrade the contract in place
body: In December 2020, S3 moved to strong read-after-write consistency without any API change and without any price change. Every existing application got stronger guarantees on the same day, with no client migration. The chapter calls this a model for "upgrade the contract in place". Similarly, ShardStore replaced earlier storage node software inside S3 behind the same API. Both changes improved the service underneath while customers kept using exactly the same interface.
deeper:
Before this change, applications that wrote an object and immediately read or listed it could see stale results, so many built workarounds: retries, extra metadata stores, or delays. After December 2020, a read after a successful write returns the new data. Those workarounds became unnecessary overnight.

Why is "in place" so valuable? The alternative, a new API or a new storage class with stronger guarantees, would have required every customer to change code and migrate data. At S3's scale, that could take years and many customers would never finish. Upgrading the existing contract delivers the benefit to everyone immediately.

The difficulty is entirely on the provider's side: strengthening guarantees under a live system serving hundreds of millions of requests per second without raising prices. That requires deep control of internals, which AWS has because it builds its own storage nodes and validates them with formal methods.

The "what to steal from AWS" list includes this directly: upgrade guarantees in place without API changes, as S3 did with strong consistency.

quiz.q: How did S3's move to strong consistency in 2020 illustrate 'upgrade the contract in place'?
quiz.a: Every existing application got stronger guarantees without API or price changes; no client code changes or migration were needed.

title: AWS migration moves: same API, new internals
body: AWS's notable storage migrations share one theme: change internals, keep the interface. S3 moved to strong consistency in 2020 with no API or price change. ShardStore replaced earlier storage node software inside S3, again behind the same API. And Amazon retail moved from Oracle to AWS databases in 2019, using AWS Database Migration Service and rewriting many schemas to fit key-value models. The first two were invisible to customers; the third required real application work.
deeper:
It is worth separating the two kinds of migration. S3's consistency upgrade and the ShardStore swap happened below a stable API. Customers did nothing, because the contract they depended on either stayed the same or got strictly better. This is the cheapest kind of migration for users and the hardest for the provider.

The Oracle exit was different. The retailer was changing the interface itself, from a relational database to purpose-built services like DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift. That meant schema rewrites and application changes across about 7,500 databases holding 75 PB. The migration service handled data movement, but the modelling work was unavoidable.

The general lesson echoes other companies in the chapter. Google moved from GFS to Colossus by keeping a client library API. Netflix built a KV abstraction layer so future backend moves become platform tasks. Uber moved bytes to Google Cloud behind an HDFS-compatible connector. When you control a stable interface, you can migrate what lies behind it without touching every user.

quiz.q: Why were S3's ShardStore swap and consistency upgrade cheaper for customers than the Oracle exit was for Amazon retail?
quiz.a: They happened behind an unchanged S3 API, so customers did nothing; the Oracle exit changed the database interface itself, forcing schema rewrites and application changes.

title: S3 encrypts by default since 2023 and keeps data in-Region
body: Since January 2023, S3 encrypts all new objects by default with S3-managed keys, called SSE-S3. Customers can choose AWS KMS keys instead for more control. On residency, data stays in the Region the customer chooses: S3 does not move it to other Regions unless the customer sets up replication. That Region guarantee is the base of most AWS data residency stories, whose mechanics Chapter 11 covers.
deeper:
Default encryption removes a common failure: a bucket created without encryption because someone forgot a setting. With SSE-S3 on by default, every new object is encrypted at rest without customer action. Choosing KMS keys instead gives the customer control over key policies, rotation and revocation, which many compliance regimes prefer.

Note the wording: all new objects since January 2023. Objects written earlier were not necessarily covered by this default, which matters for audits of older buckets.

Residency on AWS is built on a simple, strong promise: data does not leave the chosen Region unless the customer configures replication. That makes compliance reasoning straightforward: pick a Region inside the required jurisdiction and avoid cross-Region replication to outside it.

Compare with peers: Google Cloud encrypts all customer data at rest by default and offers CMEK; Azure encrypts with 256-bit AES by default, cannot be turned off, and supports customer keys. The chapter's takeaway: encryption at rest is now a default, not an option, at AWS S3 (2023), Azure Storage and Google Cloud.

quiz.q: What is the basis of most AWS data residency stories, according to the chapter?
quiz.a: S3 keeps data in the customer-chosen Region and does not move it elsewhere unless the customer sets up replication.

title: Meta's stack: Tectonic underneath, caches on top
body: Meta runs its own data centers on OCP (Open Compute Project) servers with HDD and flash. Its foundation is Tectonic, an exabyte-scale distributed file system used from about 2017 onward. Tectonic hosts a blob storage tenant, which replaced Haystack (2010) and f4 (2014), and a data warehouse tenant, which replaced HDFS. Warehouse engines are Presto, Spark and Hive. Online data lives in MySQL with MyRocks (UDB, the social graph database) and ZippyDB. Reads are absorbed by a Memcache fleet and TAO, a graph cache.
deeper:
The shape mirrors Google's: one shared file system at the bottom, many specialised systems on top. But Meta got there by a different route. Until about 2016 it ran a separate custom system per workload; from 2017 it consolidated onto Tectonic.

Key pieces in the comparison table: foundation Tectonic; object/blob layer the Tectonic blob tenant; main online databases MySQL/MyRocks and ZippyDB; caches Memcache and TAO; lake Tectonic plus Presto/Spark; archival in cold storage tiers and cold storage halls; own data centers; build and open-source.

Open source is a distinctive part of Meta's approach. It has open-sourced RocksDB, MyRocks, Presto and, originally, Cassandra.

ZippyDB plays a double role. It is a general-purpose key-value store for applications, and it also stores Tectonic's metadata, echoing how Google's Bigtable stores Colossus's metadata.

In 2024 the same foundation extended to AI: Meta's GenAI clusters use a flash-optimised version of Tectonic for checkpoints and data loading.

quiz.q: Which older systems did Tectonic's tenants replace at Meta?
quiz.a: The blob storage tenant replaced Haystack and f4; the data warehouse tenant replaced HDFS.

title: Haystack and f4: Meta's hot and warm photo stores
body: Haystack (OSDI 2010) was Meta's photo store. It packed many photos into large files to cut metadata I/O, since looking up millions of small files was the bottleneck. In 2010 it held over 260 billion images, about 20 PB, and received about 1 billion new photos (about 60 TB) per week. f4 (OSDI 2014) was a warm blob store for less-accessed photos, using Reed-Solomon (10,4) erasure coding plus XOR across data centers. In 2014 it held over 65 PB of logical warm data.
deeper:
The two systems split blobs by temperature. Recent photos are hot and read often, so Haystack kept them replicated for fast reads. Older photos are warm, read occasionally, so f4 stored them more cheaply with erasure coding.

f4's key number is its effective replication factor: 2.1 instead of 3.6. Reed-Solomon (10,4) splits data into 10 data fragments and adds 4 parity fragments, and an XOR across data centers protects against losing a whole site. The result stores far fewer bytes per logical byte than keeping full replicas.

Haystack's trick was about metadata, not durability. Storing each photo as its own file means a file system lookup per photo, which adds disk seeks. Packing many photos into large files meant far fewer files for the file system to track, cutting that metadata I/O.

Both systems later became Tectonic's blob storage tenant. The Tectonic paper explains why: each specialised system wasted a resource the other had in excess, which the next cards explain as stranded resources.

quiz.q: Why did f4 use erasure coding while Haystack kept replicas?
quiz.a: f4 held warm, rarely read photos, so cheaper Reed-Solomon coding (effective replication 2.1 vs 3.6) suited it; Haystack's hot photos needed fast reads from replicas.

title: TAO and Memcache: how Meta keeps reads off MySQL
body: TAO (USENIX ATC 2013) is a graph-aware, geographically distributed cache and store for Meta's social graph, sitting over MySQL. In 2013 it handled about a billion reads per second and millions of writes per second. Meta's 2013 NSDI paper describes how it scaled memcached into a regional, multi-cluster cache. Together, Memcache and TAO absorb most reads, so MySQL sees mostly writes and cache misses. This layered caching is how a relational database sits behind a social network.
deeper:
The read-to-write ratio is the key. The social graph (friends, likes, comments) is read vastly more than it is written: TAO's published load was about a billion reads per second versus millions of writes. Serving all those reads from MySQL would require an enormous database fleet.

TAO is graph-aware, meaning it understands objects and associations (like "user X liked post Y") rather than opaque keys. That lets it cache graph queries directly. Being geographically distributed means reads can be served close to users.

Memcache handles more general caching. The NSDI paper describes going from memcached on individual servers to a regional, multi-cluster system, which raises problems like keeping caches consistent across clusters and avoiding overload when many clients miss at once.

With both layers in place, MySQL's job narrows to durable storage of writes and occasional reads on cache misses. Meta later changed MySQL's storage engine (to MyRocks) precisely because the database was bound by storage space rather than by CPU or I/O, which fits a database shielded from most reads.

quiz.q: Why can Meta run its huge social graph on MySQL?
quiz.a: Memcache and TAO absorb most reads (TAO: about a billion reads per second), so MySQL mainly handles writes and cache misses.

title: MyRocks and ZippyDB: Meta's RocksDB-based databases
body: MyRocks is MySQL with the RocksDB storage engine, which is based on an LSM (log-structured merge) tree. Meta migrated UDB, its social graph database, to MyRocks in 2017, halving UDB's storage. ZippyDB, described in 2021, is a general-purpose, strongly consistent key-value store built on RocksDB with Paxos replication. Both reuse RocksDB, Meta's open-source single-node storage engine, and add replication and interfaces on top. ZippyDB also stores Tectonic's metadata.
deeper:
RocksDB underpins both because LSM trees write data sequentially and compress well, which suits flash and reduces space. That compression was the entire reason for MyRocks: UDB was space-bound on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle, and MyRocks compresses much better than InnoDB, MySQL's default engine.

ZippyDB adds Paxos, a consensus protocol, on top of RocksDB so that replicas agree on writes and reads can be strongly consistent. That makes it suitable for critical metadata, which is exactly how Tectonic uses it: Tectonic's Name, File and Block metadata layers are hash-partitioned and stored in ZippyDB.

The pattern is similar to Uber building Schemaless and Docstore on MySQL, and to LinkedIn building Espresso on MySQL: keep a well-tested single-node engine and put the company's effort into sharding, replication and APIs. Meta's twist is that it wrote the engine itself (RocksDB) and open-sourced it.

The InnoDB-to-MyRocks migration is also one of the chapter's model migrations, covered separately.

quiz.q: Why did Meta move UDB from InnoDB to MyRocks?
quiz.a: UDB was space-bound on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle; MyRocks' LSM-based RocksDB engine compresses much better, halving UDB's storage.

title: Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for many tenants
body: Tectonic, described at FAST in 2021, is Meta's single exabyte-scale distributed file system for many tenants. It replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS. In 2021, one multitenant production cluster had 1,590 PB of capacity with 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files, 15 billion blocks and 4,208 storage nodes. Moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10x. It is the same foundation-first move Google made with Colossus.
deeper:
The numbers show the point of consolidation. A single cluster holding 1,250 PB for multiple tenants means blob storage and warehouse data share disks. Fewer, larger clusters mean less duplicated overhead and better pooling of capacity and IOPS.

The 10x cut in warehouse clusters is especially telling. HDFS clusters are limited by the single NameNode's metadata capacity (Chapter 2), so a large warehouse needs many separate HDFS clusters. Tectonic's disaggregated metadata, split into Name, File and Block layers stored in ZippyDB, removes that limit, so far fewer clusters are needed.

The paper says Tectonic had run in single-tenant clusters "for several years, completely replacing Haystack, f4, and HDFS" by 2021. So the migration was gradual: first prove the system tenant by tenant, then combine tenants.

In the side-by-side table, Tectonic's figure is "1,590 PB capacity in one multitenant cluster" (2021). That is a single-cluster capacity, not Meta's total storage, so compare it carefully with fleet-wide figures like S3's hundreds of exabytes.

quiz.q: Why did moving the warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut warehouse clusters by 10x?
quiz.a: HDFS clusters are capped by one NameNode's metadata; Tectonic shards metadata into ZippyDB, so one cluster can grow far larger and fewer clusters are needed.

title: Meta's arc: specialize first, then consolidate
body: Meta's storage history follows a clear arc. From 2010 to 2016 it specialised, building a custom system per workload: Haystack for hot photos, f4 for warm photos, HDFS for the warehouse. From 2017 onward it consolidated onto one distributed file system, Tectonic, for all of them. Meta builds its own systems, open-sources many (RocksDB, MyRocks, Presto, Cassandra originally) and runs its own data centers. The consolidation reason was efficiency: separate systems wasted resources.
deeper:
Specialisation made sense at first. Each workload had distinct needs, and building a dedicated system let engineers learn the workload deeply and optimise for it: Haystack for fast photo lookups, f4 for cheap warm storage, HDFS for batch analytics.

But specialised systems each carry their own disk fleet, and the Tectonic paper shows what that costs. Each fleet ends up bottlenecked on a different resource, so each has slack in the resource the other needs. One shared system can pack tenants with different needs onto the same disks.

This arc also explains why Meta's stack looks like Google's today even though its history differs. Google standardised on GFS and Colossus early; Meta arrived at the same single-foundation design about ten years later, after learning its workloads.

The chapter treats "specialize, then consolidate" as a general pattern, restated in the key takeaways: stranded IOPS and stranded capacity are the signal to consolidate. The same philosophy continued in 2024, when AI training storage was built on a flash-optimised Tectonic rather than a new system.

quiz.q: Why does specialisation tend to win early in a company's storage history?
quiz.a: Dedicated systems let engineers learn each workload and optimise for it; the cost of separate fleets only dominates later, at larger scale.

title: Stranded resources: why Haystack's replication hit 5.3x
body: The Tectonic paper gives a sharp reason for consolidation: specialised systems strand resources. Haystack was IOPS-bound: it had spare disk space but not enough I/O, so extra disks were added for I/O, and its effective replication factor climbed from an ideal 3.6x to 5.3x. f4 had the opposite problem: lots of spare IOPS and less space. Two systems each wasted the resource the other needed. One shared system can pack IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants onto the same disks.
deeper:
Every disk provides two things: capacity (bytes) and IOPS (input/output operations per second). A workload uses both in some ratio. Hot photos generate many reads per byte, so Haystack ran out of IOPS long before it filled its disks. To get more I/O, Meta added disks, which added capacity it did not need. That unused capacity showed up as an effective replication factor of 5.3x instead of the designed 3.6x: more raw bytes per logical byte than the durability scheme required.

f4 held warm photos that are rarely read, so it used little I/O per byte. Its disks filled up with plenty of I/O left over.

Put both tenants on the same disks and the imbalance cancels. Hot data uses the IOPS that warm data leaves idle; warm data uses the space hot data leaves empty. That is the efficiency gain Tectonic captured.

This is the answer to the chapter's first check-your-understanding question, and the warning sign to look for in your own fleets: one bound by IOPS while another with the same disks is bound by capacity.

quiz.q: Why did Haystack's effective replication factor rise from 3.6x to 5.3x, and how did Tectonic solve it?
quiz.a: Haystack was IOPS-bound, so disks were added for I/O, leaving capacity idle. Tectonic pooled Haystack-like and f4-like tenants on shared disks, balancing IOPS and capacity needs.

title: Senior staff lens: the warning sign that says consolidate
body: Senior staff lens: "specialize, then consolidate" is a common arc. Specialisation wins early because you learn the workload. Consolidation wins later because stranded capacity becomes the biggest cost. The warning sign is exactly Meta's: one fleet is bound by IOPS while another fleet with the same disks is bound by capacity. When you see that pattern in your own infrastructure, pooling the fleets can reclaim the wasted resource on both sides.
deeper:
The timing matters. Consolidating too early forces one generic system onto workloads nobody fully understands yet, and the shared system may be poorly tuned for all of them. Consolidating too late means paying for idle IOPS in one fleet and idle bytes in another, at a scale where that waste is the largest line item.

How would you detect the signal? Track, per fleet, which resource runs out first. If a fleet buys hardware because it lacks IOPS while its disks are half full, it is IOPS-bound. If another buys hardware because disks are full while I/O is low, it is capacity-bound. Two such fleets on the same disk type are a consolidation opportunity.

Consolidation has costs too: noisy neighbours, a bigger blast radius and a harder migration. Meta handled the migration gradually, running Tectonic in single-tenant clusters for years before replacing Haystack, f4 and HDFS. And Azure's storage stamps show the opposite answer to how big one failure domain should be, which is discussed in the Microsoft section.

quiz.q: What is the risk of consolidating storage systems too early?
quiz.a: You force one generic system onto workloads you don't yet understand, so it may serve all of them poorly; specialisation first teaches you the workloads.

title: Tectonic's disaggregated metadata, stored in ZippyDB
body: Tectonic scales by disaggregating metadata. It splits file system metadata into three layers: Name (the directory tree and file names), File (which blocks make up each file) and Block (where each block's data lives). Each layer is hash-partitioned and stored in ZippyDB, Meta's Paxos-replicated key-value store. No single master holds all metadata, so metadata capacity grows by adding partitions. This is the same idea as Google's Colossus storing metadata in Bigtable.
deeper:
Splitting metadata into layers lets each part scale and be partitioned independently. Name-layer operations like listing a directory touch different data than block-location lookups during reads, so separating them spreads load across different partitions.

Hash partitioning distributes entries evenly across ZippyDB shards, avoiding hotspots where one shard holds a popular directory's entire subtree. Storing metadata in ZippyDB also means Tectonic inherits Paxos replication and strong consistency without building its own consensus.

Why this matters so much: metadata scaling drove the biggest storage redesigns in this chapter. GFS broke because one master held all metadata in RAM; HDFS has the same single-NameNode limit, which LinkedIn still works hard to manage. Both Google and Meta solved it the same way: move metadata into a sharded key-value store they already operate.

The practical effect at Meta was visible in the warehouse: moving from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10x, because clusters no longer needed to be small enough for one metadata server.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic hash-partition its metadata layers across ZippyDB?
quiz.a: Hashing spreads metadata evenly across shards, so no single master or hot partition limits the file system, and metadata capacity grows by adding partitions.

title: One file system, different durability recipes per tenant
body: In Tectonic, the client library does the encoding, so each tenant chooses its own durability recipe. Blob storage writes data replicated first, then re-encodes it to Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) once a block is sealed. The data warehouse uses RS(9,6) for long-lived data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle data. One distributed file system thus serves very different workloads, each with the encoding that fits its write pattern and lifetime, without separate storage clusters.
deeper:
Why replicate first and encode later for blobs? Blob writes arrive as small appends. Erasure coding works on complete blocks, so encoding each small append would be expensive. Replicating while a block is still being written keeps appends cheap and fast; once the block is sealed (complete and immutable), it is re-encoded to RS(10,4), which stores far less overhead than full replicas.

The warehouse makes different choices. Long-lived tables use RS(9,6), which tolerates more fragment losses, fitting data that must survive for a long time. Shuffle data, the temporary intermediate output passed between stages of a job, lives briefly, so RS(3,3) gives adequate protection with simpler encoding.

This mirrors Colossus, whose client library does software RAID and erasure coding so each application picks its durability and performance mix. The "what to steal from Meta" list phrases it as: let each tenant pick its encoding (replicate-then-re-encode for small appends, RS for sealed data).

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic's blob tenant replicate data first and erasure-code it only after a block is sealed?
quiz.a: Blob writes are small appends; erasure coding needs complete blocks, so replication keeps appends cheap, then sealed immutable blocks are re-encoded to RS(10,4) to cut overhead.

title: InnoDB to MyRocks: a migration you could always roll back
body: In 2017 Meta moved UDB, its social graph database, from MySQL's InnoDB engine to MyRocks. MyRocks instances first joined as replicas, were validated with checksums and shadow queries, then promoted to primary. Because InnoDB and MyRocks could replicate each other, rollback was always possible. The motivation was that UDB was space-bound on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle, and MyRocks compresses much better. The result halved UDB's storage.
deeper:
Each step reduced risk. Joining as replicas meant MyRocks received real production writes without serving production reads yet. Checksums compared data between InnoDB and MyRocks replicas to prove the new engine stored exactly the same data. Shadow queries sent real read traffic to MyRocks and compared results, catching behavioural differences before users could see them. Only after that was a MyRocks instance promoted to primary.

The key property was bidirectional replication. If a problem appeared after promotion, an InnoDB replica could be promoted back, because it had kept receiving changes. The migration was never a one-way door.

The chapter's key takeaways group this with Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit: good migrations are reversible and change one thing at a time, using dual running and gradual cutover. The "what to steal from Meta" list says: migrate engines with dual replication and checksums so you can always roll back.

Note the change was only the storage engine; MySQL, replication and applications stayed the same.

quiz.q: What made Meta's InnoDB-to-MyRocks migration reversible at every step?
quiz.a: InnoDB and MyRocks could replicate each other, so a former InnoDB replica stayed current and could be promoted back if MyRocks misbehaved.

title: From Haystack to Tectonic to AI training storage
body: Meta's other big migration moved Haystack, f4 and HDFS onto Tectonic. The Tectonic paper says that by 2021 Tectonic had run in single-tenant clusters "for several years, completely replacing Haystack, f4, and HDFS". In 2024, Meta's GenAI clusters extended the same foundation: they use a FUSE API backed by a flash-optimised version of Tectonic for checkpoints and data loading, plus a Hammerspace parallel NFS for interactive work. Same foundation, new hardware tier.
deeper:
The Tectonic rollout was staged. Running single-tenant clusters first meant each old system's workload could move onto Tectonic and be proven on its own before tenants were combined into multitenant clusters, where the efficiency gains from pooling come in.

The AI extension shows the payoff of owning a strong foundation. AI training has different needs: very fast reads for loading training data and large, fast writes for checkpoints, the periodic saves of model state. Instead of a brand-new storage system, Meta built a flash-optimised version of Tectonic. FUSE, a way of exposing storage as a normal file system to programs, lets training code read and write files without special client libraries.

Where Tectonic did not fit, interactive work, Meta used Hammerspace parallel NFS, a separate system. That is a pragmatic mix: extend the core foundation for the heavy path and use something else for a different access pattern.

The pattern echoes the chapter's recurring theme: shared foundation at the bottom, workload-specific pieces on top, and new hardware tiers added inside the foundation.

quiz.q: How did Meta support GenAI training storage in 2024 without building an entirely new foundation?
quiz.a: It used a flash-optimised Tectonic behind a FUSE API for checkpoints and data loading, adding Hammerspace parallel NFS only for interactive work.

title: Messenger's default E2EE changed what storage can do
body: Meta made end-to-end encryption the default for Messenger in December 2023. End-to-end encryption means only the communicating devices hold the keys. This changes storage design: the server stores ciphertext it cannot read, so server-side search and indexing of message content are no longer possible. Any feature that needs to understand message content must move to the device. Chapter 11 covers the storage consequences of this shift in detail.
deeper:
With ordinary encryption at rest, the provider encrypts data on disk but holds the keys, so its servers can still decrypt, search, index and process content. End-to-end encryption removes that ability entirely. The server becomes a store of opaque bytes.

For storage engineers, that has concrete effects. Server-side full-text search over messages cannot work. Content-based indexing, deduplication based on content, and server-side processing of message text are no longer possible. Search, if offered, must run on the user's device over locally decrypted data.

Apple's Advanced Data Protection, launched in 2022, has the same effect for iCloud: users can turn on end-to-end encryption for most iCloud data categories, so Apple does not hold the keys.

The chapter's key takeaways contrast these: encryption at rest is now a default at AWS S3, Azure Storage and Google Cloud, but end-to-end encryption, as at Meta Messenger and Apple ADP, changes what the server can do with stored data. It is a product and architecture decision, not just a security setting.

quiz.q: Why does default end-to-end encryption in Messenger rule out server-side message search?
quiz.a: The server stores only ciphertext and never holds the keys, so it cannot read, index or search message content; such features must run on devices.

title: Azure's stack: storage stamps with three layers
body: Windows Azure Storage (WAS), described at SOSP in 2011, organises storage into "storage stamps": fixed-size units of racks of storage nodes. Each stamp has three layers. A front-end layer receives requests. A partition layer serves tables, blobs, queues and indexes. A stream layer stores data as append-only extents protected with LRC erasure coding. On this sit Blob Storage, ADLS Gen2, Managed Disks (page blobs), Azure SQL Hyperscale, Cosmos DB and Azure Cache for Redis. Archival uses an Archive tier, with research on Project Silica glass.
deeper:
The stream layer is Azure's foundation, equivalent in role to Colossus at Google or Tectonic at Meta: it turns disks into durable, append-only storage. The partition layer gives that foundation different data abstractions (blobs, tables, queues) and indexes them. Front ends route requests to the right partition.

Managed Disks, the virtual machine disks, are page blobs, so even block storage for VMs is built on the same stamp architecture.

In the comparison table, Azure's foundation is "stream layer in stamps"; object layer Blob and ADLS Gen2; main online databases Cosmos DB and Azure SQL; cache Azure Cache for Redis; lake ADLS plus Synapse/Fabric; archival Archive tier with Silica research; cloud status "is the cloud"; build vs buy "build core, buy companies".

The difference from Google and Meta is the unit of growth. Instead of one giant cluster per region, Azure adds whole stamps. Growth, rebalancing and failure isolation all revolve around stamps, as the following cards explain.

quiz.q: Which layer of a Windows Azure Storage stamp plays the role that Colossus plays at Google?
quiz.a: The stream layer: it stores data as append-only extents with LRC erasure coding, forming the durable foundation beneath the partition and front-end layers.

title: Local Reconstruction Codes: cheaper repairs than Reed-Solomon
body: Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC), presented at USENIX ATC in 2012, are the erasure code Azure uses in its stream layer. An erasure code stores data fragments plus parity fragments so lost pieces can be rebuilt. LRC's advantage: it repairs a single lost fragment by reading fewer fragments than Reed-Solomon needs. LRC reduced storage overhead compared with triple replication while keeping repair reads low. At Azure's size, a small cut in storage overhead is a very large saving.
deeper:
Repair cost matters because single-fragment losses are by far the most common failure: one disk or one node fails. With standard Reed-Solomon, rebuilding one lost fragment typically requires reading many other fragments, which consumes network bandwidth and disk I/O across the cluster. LRC groups fragments locally so a single loss can be rebuilt from a smaller local group, cutting repair reads.

The overhead side is the money. Triple replication stores 3 bytes for every logical byte. Erasure codes store much less. Across a fleet the size of Azure's, even a few percentage points less overhead means huge amounts of hardware not bought, which Chapter 12 quantifies.
