This is why the "what to steal from Azure" list says: invest in erasure codes, because small overhead cuts are large savings at scale. Meta made a similar bet with f4, whose Reed-Solomon (10,4) plus XOR design brought effective replication to 2.1 instead of 3.6.

The trade-off, as always with erasure coding, is more computation and more complex repair logic than simple replication.

quiz.q: What problem does LRC solve compared with standard Reed-Solomon coding?
quiz.a: It rebuilds a single lost fragment, the most common failure, by reading fewer fragments, cutting repair I/O and network cost while keeping low storage overhead.

title: Cosmos DB, Socrates, ADLS Gen2 and Project Silica
body: Azure's other key systems each fill a layer. Cosmos DB, generally available in 2017, is a globally distributed, multi-model database with five consistency levels. Socrates, the design behind Azure SQL Hyperscale (SIGMOD 2019), splits SQL Server into compute, a log service and page servers over Azure Storage. ADLS Gen2 (2019) is Blob Storage plus a real hierarchical namespace for analytics. Project Silica, research from 2019 onward, stores data in quartz glass for very long archival life.
deeper:
Cosmos DB's five consistency levels let applications choose between strong consistency and weaker, faster, more available options, a spectrum rather than a binary choice.

Socrates follows the same principle as AWS Aurora: separate compute from storage. By moving the log into its own service and pages onto page servers, compute nodes scale on their own and database storage can grow past one machine. The chapter lists "split compute from storage in databases" as one of Azure's scaling techniques.

ADLS Gen2 matters for analytics. Plain object stores have flat namespaces, so renaming a "directory" means renaming every object under it, which is slow and not atomic. A real hierarchical namespace makes rename and directory operations atomic and fast, which analytics engines depend on when they commit output.

Project Silica is at the far end of archival: storing data in quartz glass for very long life. It is listed as research, not a production service, and the comparison table notes "Silica research" in Azure's archival column next to the production Archive tier.

quiz.q: Why does a hierarchical namespace (ADLS Gen2) matter for analytics workloads?
quiz.a: It makes rename and directory operations atomic and fast, unlike flat object stores where renaming a directory means slowly renaming every object under it.

title: Azure's published scale and the 70 percent stamp ceiling
body: The 2011 WAS paper reported 70 PB of raw storage in production, with a few hundred more PB being provisioned. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw; next-generation stamps held up to 30 PB. Each stamp is kept around 70 percent utilized. When a stamp nears that level, the location service moves accounts to other stamps. Microsoft has not published a current exabyte total for Azure Storage as a single figure, so the chapter gives none.
deeper:
The 70 percent ceiling is a deliberate buffer. A stamp that runs near full has no room to absorb failures (rebuilding lost data needs free space), sudden customer growth or rebalancing. Keeping headroom makes each stamp safer and more predictable.

The location service is what makes the ceiling practical. It knows which stamp holds each storage account, and it can move accounts between stamps using inter-stamp replication. So rather than one stamp growing without bound, load is redistributed across the fleet.

The growth from about 2 PB to up to 30 PB per stamp shows stamps are fixed-size within a generation, while the size of a stamp can change between generations.

In the side-by-side table, Azure WAS appears as "70 PB raw, stamps up to 30 PB" (2011). That is a 2011 number and much older than most others in the table, which the chapter warns about: published numbers differ in kind and year. It says nothing about Azure's current size.

The "what to steal from Azure" list distils this: make the unit of growth a fixed-size stamp, keep it below a utilization ceiling, and move accounts between stamps.

quiz.q: Why keep each Azure storage stamp around 70 percent utilized rather than filling it?
quiz.a: Headroom absorbs failures, repairs and customer growth; when a stamp nears the ceiling, the location service moves accounts to other stamps.

title: Microsoft's philosophy: build the core, grow by stamps
body: Microsoft builds its core cloud storage and also buys companies and products. For example, it owns LinkedIn and GitHub, which keep their own stacks. Azure's defining design choice is the storage stamp: a fixed-size unit of racks with its own partition and stream layers. Growth means adding stamps, not growing one giant cluster. Azure scales by stamps and rebalances by moving accounts between stamps with inter-stamp replication.
deeper:
The acquisitions point is a notable contrast with Google. Google's internal systems largely share one foundation. Microsoft lets acquired companies keep their own infrastructure: LinkedIn still runs its own data centers with HDFS, Espresso and Venice. In 2019 LinkedIn announced a plan to move to Azure, but paused it in 2022, citing the value of its existing on-prem investment.

Stamps are an operational philosophy. Because each stamp is a self-contained unit, capacity planning becomes a matter of counting stamps. A failure or bad deployment is naturally contained within one stamp. And the design scales linearly: need more capacity, add more stamps.

Beyond stamps, Azure scales with better erasure codes (LRC) to cut storage cost, and by splitting compute from storage in databases (Socrates), so compute nodes scale on their own and storage grows past one machine.

The cost of stamps is the flip side of Meta's giant clusters: resources can be stranded in individual stamps, and rebalancing requires moving accounts. The next card frames this as a deliberate trade-off about failure domain size.

quiz.q: How does Azure add storage capacity, and what makes capacity planning simple as a result?
quiz.a: It adds whole fixed-size stamps instead of growing one cluster, so capacity planning becomes counting stamps, with accounts moved between stamps to rebalance.

title: Senior staff lens: stamps vs giant clusters
body: Senior staff lens: Azure's stamps and Meta's exabyte clusters are opposite answers to the same question: how big should one storage failure domain be? Stamps keep the blast radius small and turn capacity planning into counting stamps. Giant clusters reduce stranded capacity by pooling resources. There is no universal right answer. Ask which cost dominates for you: outage scope or wasted capacity. That question, not fashion, should decide the size of your storage units.
deeper:
The trade-off in detail: with stamps, if one stamp has spare IOPS and another spare bytes, they cannot easily share, so capacity strands across stamps, and rebalancing requires account moves between stamps. With a giant cluster, resources pool naturally, which is exactly the efficiency Meta chased by consolidating Haystack, f4 and HDFS onto Tectonic. But a bad failure or bad deployment in a giant cluster can affect much more data.

Which cost dominates depends on the business. A public cloud serving many external customers may weigh outage scope heavily, since one incident can hit many customers at once. An internal platform with enormous, well-understood workloads may weigh wasted hardware more.

This connects to AWS's cell-based architecture, which also splits services so one failure hits only a slice of customers (Chapter 10).

This is the chapter's sixth check-your-understanding question: stamps limit blast radius and simplify capacity planning but can strand capacity and need account moves; giant clusters pool resources better but risk wider impact.

quiz.q: What does Azure's storage stamp design trade away compared with Meta's exabyte-scale clusters?
quiz.a: Stamps give small blast radius and simple capacity planning but can strand capacity across stamps and need account moves; giant clusters pool better but failures hit more data.

title: ADLS Gen2: migrate by adding a capability, not a system
body: Microsoft's most visible storage change was adding a hierarchical namespace to Blob Storage, creating ADLS Gen2, instead of running a separate file system for analytics. Users kept one storage account; the namespace made rename and directory operations atomic and fast. The chapter calls this a migration by adding a capability to the existing system rather than building a new system next to it. Data did not have to move between two separate storage products.
deeper:
The alternative would have been a standalone analytics file system beside Blob Storage. Customers would then have to copy data between the two, manage two sets of permissions and pay for duplicate storage. Adding the namespace to Blob Storage avoided all that: the same account and the same data could serve both object-style applications and analytics engines.

Why do analytics engines need a hierarchical namespace? Jobs often write output to a temporary directory and rename it into place to commit. On a flat object store, "renaming a directory" means copying and deleting every object under the prefix, which is slow and can leave partial results if interrupted. With a real namespace, the rename is a single atomic metadata operation.

This is the same spirit as S3's strong consistency upgrade: improve the existing system in place so users benefit without migrating. It also echoes the comparison table's lake column for Azure: ADLS plus Synapse and Fabric, the analytics engines that read from it.

quiz.q: Why was adding a hierarchical namespace to Blob Storage better than building a separate analytics file system?
quiz.a: Users kept one storage account and one copy of data, avoiding copies between systems, while gaining atomic, fast rename and directory operations.

title: Azure encryption can't be turned off; EU data stays in the EU
body: Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest by default with 256-bit AES, and this encryption cannot be turned off. Customers can bring their own keys. For residency, Microsoft's EU Data Boundary commits to storing and processing EU customer data within the EU for its core cloud services, and Microsoft has published documentation on the boundary. These are Azure's published compliance positions; Chapter 11 covers the underlying mechanics of keys and residency.
deeper:
"Cannot be turned off" is a stronger statement than "on by default". It means there is no configuration in which Azure Storage holds unencrypted data at rest, so no audit has to check for disabled encryption. Bring-your-own-key gives customers control over the key, enabling rotation and revocation under their own policies.

The EU Data Boundary goes beyond regional storage. Region choice alone says where data is stored; the boundary also commits to processing EU customer data within the EU for core cloud services. That matters for regulations that care about where data is accessed and handled, not only where it rests.

Compare the three big clouds. Google Cloud encrypts all customer data at rest by default and offers CMEK, with residency via regions and Assured Workloads. AWS S3 encrypts all new objects by default since January 2023 with SSE-S3 or optional KMS keys, and keeps data in the chosen Region unless replication is configured. Azure encrypts with AES-256 that cannot be disabled, supports customer keys, and offers the EU Data Boundary.

quiz.q: How does the EU Data Boundary go further than simply choosing an EU region?
quiz.a: It commits to both storing and processing EU customer data within the EU for core cloud services, not just where the data rests.

title: Uber's stack: thin layers on MySQL, HDFS and open source
body: Uber historically ran its own data centers and is moving to Oracle Cloud and Google Cloud. Its online stack is a MySQL fleet with Schemaless (2016), which evolved into Docstore, plus Cassandra. Redis caches called CacheFront sit in front of Docstore. Analytics uses HDFS, with over 1 EB per region and moving to Google Cloud Storage, and a lake of Apache Hudi tables with Hive, Presto and Spark. Colder data is kept in cheaper storage. In 2016 Uber moved core storage from Postgres to MySQL.
deeper:
The 2016 Postgres-to-MySQL move is one of the best-known public database switches. Uber cited write amplification and replication issues with Postgres. Write amplification means each logical update causes much more physical writing, which hurts at high update rates. MySQL then became the base for Uber's custom storage layers.

Schemaless (2016) was an append-only, sharded datastore on MySQL. It later evolved into Docstore, publicly described in 2020 as a general-purpose document database: MySQL per node, Raft replication, and strict serializability per partition. Raft is a consensus protocol that keeps replicas in agreement.

Apache Hudi, created at Uber in 2016 to 2017, adds upserts and incremental reads on HDFS and is now an Apache project.

In the comparison table, Uber's foundation is HDFS moving to GCS; object storage is HDFS or cloud object storage; online databases are Docstore (MySQL) and Cassandra; cache Redis (CacheFront); lake Hudi, Hive, Presto; archival cheaper tiers; cloud status moving to OCI and GCP; build vs buy thin layers on open source.

quiz.q: Why did Uber move its core storage from Postgres to MySQL in 2016?
quiz.a: Uber cited write amplification and replication issues with Postgres.

title: Hudi: Uber's fix for rewriting whole tables every day
body: Apache Hudi was created at Uber in 2016 to 2017 to support upserts (update-or-insert) and incremental reads on HDFS. It is now an Apache project. Before tools like Hudi, a data lake table often had to be rewritten entirely each day to reflect changes. With Hudi, jobs write only changed records, and downstream jobs read only what changed since their last run. This incremental processing, covered in Chapter 7, saves enormous compute and storage I/O at Uber's scale.
deeper:
The problem Hudi solves comes from how lakes store data: immutable files on a distributed file system. Changing one record in an immutable file means rewriting the file, and without an index of which file holds which record, jobs often rewrote whole tables or partitions. For a company whose trips, payments and driver states change constantly, that is expensive and slow, and data freshness suffers.

Hudi adds a layer that tracks records and file versions, so updates can be applied to just the affected files and readers can ask for changes since a point in time. That makes pipelines incremental rather than full-recompute.

Hudi fits Uber's philosophy of thin custom layers on proven engines: it sits on HDFS and Parquet rather than replacing them. It is analogous to Netflix's Iceberg and LinkedIn's move to Iceberg, which also added table-level metadata on top of files in object or file storage.

Uber's scale makes the savings concrete: its 2024 post reports more than 1 exabyte of Hadoop data across tens of thousands of servers in each of two regions.

quiz.q: How does Hudi reduce work compared with rewriting lake tables every day?
quiz.a: It supports upserts and incremental reads, so jobs write only changed records and downstream jobs read only changes since their last run.

title: Uber's published scale: Docstore and exabyte Hadoop
body: Uber published two headline storage figures. Docstore, per a 2020 blog, handles tens of millions of queries per second with availability of 99.99 percent or more and tens of petabytes of operational data. Uber's Hadoop platform, per a 2024 post, holds more than 1 exabyte of data across tens of thousands of servers in each of two regions. The first is operational (online) data serving live app traffic; the second is analytics and ML data.
deeper:
The two numbers describe very different workloads. Docstore's tens of petabytes are online data: trips, users and other records that the app reads and writes in real time, where availability of 99.99 percent or more is the key target. Hadoop's exabyte per region is batch analytics and ML data, where throughput and cost per byte matter more than per-request latency.

The ratio is typical: analytics data is often far larger than operational data, because it keeps history, copies and derived tables.

The Hadoop figure explains why Uber's move to Google Cloud needed such a careful plan. Migrating over an exabyte per region cannot be done in one step; the chapter describes it as a template for moving an exabyte.

In the side-by-side table, Uber Hadoop is "over 1 EB in each of two regions" (2024) and Uber Docstore is "tens of PB, tens of millions of QPS" (2020). Note the four-year gap between the two, again a reminder to compare numbers with the year in mind.

quiz.q: Why do Uber's Docstore and Hadoop figures differ so much in size?
quiz.a: Docstore holds live operational data (tens of PB); Hadoop holds analytics and ML data with history and derived tables, over 1 EB per region.

title: Uber's philosophy: thin custom layers on proven engines
body: Uber historically built on open source and ran its own data centers. It tends to write a thin custom layer on a proven engine: Schemaless and Docstore sit on MySQL; Hudi sits on HDFS and Parquet. This keeps the hard part, a durable single-node storage engine, in well-tested code and puts Uber's effort into sharding, replication and APIs. Since 2023 Uber has moved toward public cloud, with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud both announced as partners.
deeper:
Writing a new storage engine from scratch is one of the riskiest things an infrastructure team can do: durability bugs can lose data, and it takes years to mature. MySQL and HDFS have been hardened by enormous numbers of users. By building on them, Uber inherits that maturity and spends its engineering on what is specific to Uber: scaling out across many machines, replication across zones, and the APIs its application teams need.

Docstore is a good example of what the thin layer can add: Raft replication, strict serializability per partition, partitions spread across zones, and features like materialized views and change data capture. MySQL still handles storing rows on each node.

The move toward public cloud is a newer chapter. Uber's 2024 data platform post is explicit that the lake is moving to Google Cloud. That shift keeps the thin-layer philosophy: the first phase runs Uber's existing Hadoop stack on cloud VMs over Google Cloud Storage.

The "what to steal from Uber" list includes: build thin layers on proven engines like MySQL.

quiz.q: What does Uber gain by building Docstore on MySQL instead of writing its own storage engine?
quiz.a: It keeps durable single-node storage in well-tested code and spends its effort on sharding, replication and APIs, avoiding the risk of a new engine.

title: Docstore scales by partitions, with built-in views and CDC
body: Uber scales Docstore by partitioning everything. Data is split into partitions of 3 to 5 nodes spread across availability zones, each running MySQL and replicated with Raft. Docstore also offers materialized views and change data capture (CDC), so teams can read data by a second key without building their own pipelines. In the lake, Uber scales with incremental processing through Hudi: instead of rewriting whole tables every day, it writes only changed records (Chapter 7).
deeper:
Spreading each partition's 3 to 5 nodes across zones means a zone failure leaves each partition with a majority of replicas elsewhere, so Raft can keep accepting writes. Adding capacity means adding partitions.

Materialized views and CDC solve a common problem. Data is stored by one primary key, say a trip ID, but some teams need to look it up by another key, say a driver ID. Without built-in support, each team builds its own pipeline to copy and re-index the data, which is error-prone and duplicates effort. Docstore provides a materialized view (a maintained copy organised by the second key) and a stream of changes, so teams just use them.

This contrasts with Pinterest's cautionary tale: building secondary indexes in application code on a store without transactions led to data and index disagreeing after failures. Having the database maintain views centrally avoids each team reinventing that fragile logic.

Hudi applies the same incremental mindset to analytics: process only what changed rather than everything.

quiz.q: Why does Docstore offer materialized views and change data capture built in?
quiz.a: So teams can read data by a second key without building their own copy-and-index pipelines, avoiding duplicated, error-prone work.

title: Uber's GCP move: a template for migrating an exabyte
body: Uber's migration of its data lake to Google Cloud, announced in 2024, is a template for moving an exabyte. Step one: move bytes first and keep the software. Data goes to Google Cloud Storage while the existing Hadoop stack runs on cloud VMs; a cloud storage connector gives HDFS compatibility, so jobs do not change. Step two: federate access with proxies that route each read on-prem or to cloud. Step three: replicate both directions during transition with HiveSync. Step four: only then modernize to Dataproc and BigQuery.
deeper:
Each step removes a specific risk. Keeping the Hadoop stack while moving bytes means only the storage location changes; if something goes wrong, the software is familiar and the problem is isolated to storage. The HDFS-compatible connector hides the change from jobs entirely.

Data access proxies solve the "where does this dataset live today?" problem. During a long migration, some datasets are on-prem and some in the cloud. Proxies route each read correctly, so users do not need to track migration progress.

Bidirectional replication with HiveSync means both sides stay usable, so workloads can move back and forth and nothing is stranded during cutover.

Only after the bytes are safely in the cloud does Uber replace engines with managed services such as Dataproc and BigQuery.

This answers the chapter's fifth check-your-understanding question: the two-phase approach is safer than moving straight to BigQuery because it changes one variable at a time, the storage location first behind a compatible connector, then the engines, and each step can be rolled back independently.

quiz.q: Why is Uber's two-phase GCP migration safer than moving straight to BigQuery?
quiz.a: It changes one variable at a time: storage location first behind an HDFS-compatible connector, then engines. Each step can be rolled back independently.

title: Senior staff lens: never change storage and engines together
body: Senior staff lens: notice what Uber did not do. It did not change the storage system and the compute engines at the same time. Changing one variable at a time makes each step reversible: if problems appear, you know which change caused them and can undo just that step. Chapter 9 calls this "lift, then shift". Separately, Uber has not published a detailed storage-level compliance design in the sources used, so the chapter does not describe one.
deeper:
Why does changing two things at once hurt? If you move data to a new storage system and switch to new query engines simultaneously, and results come out wrong or slow, you cannot tell whether the storage or the engine is at fault. Rolling back means undoing both. Debugging becomes guesswork, and the migration stalls.

"Lift, then shift" means first lift the workload onto new infrastructure with minimal change (Uber: same Hadoop software on cloud VMs, reading GCS through an HDFS-compatible connector), then shift it to new, cloud-native technology (Dataproc, BigQuery) once the first step is stable.

The chapter's key takeaways generalise this: good migrations are reversible and change one thing at a time, and Meta's MyRocks move, Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit all used dual running and gradual cutover. Abstraction layers help too: Uber's HDFS-compatible cloud connector, like Netflix's KV layer, hides where bytes live.

The compliance note illustrates the chapter's accuracy rule: no published source, no description.

quiz.q: Why does changing storage and compute engines at the same time make a migration riskier?
quiz.a: When problems appear you cannot tell which change caused them, and rolling back means undoing both; one change at a time keeps each step diagnosable and reversible.

title: Netflix's stack: AWS for everything, plus its own CDN
body: Netflix runs on AWS, after migrating there from its own data centers between 2008 and January 2016, plus Open Connect, its own CDN appliances placed inside ISPs (internet service providers) to serve video. S3 holds video masters and data warehouse files. Cassandra, used from about 2010, is the main online store. EVCache, a memcached-based cross-region cache, was open-sourced in 2013. The lake uses Apache Iceberg tables with Spark and Trino. Archival uses S3 colder classes. A data abstraction layer offers KV and TimeSeries services.
deeper:
Cassandra was chosen for multi-region, always-writable replication: any region can accept writes, which suits a global streaming service that must keep working when a region has trouble.

Open Connect, launched in 2012, is the one piece of infrastructure Netflix builds at the hardware level. Its appliances sit inside ISPs, so video bytes travel a short distance to viewers.

Apache Iceberg was created at Netflix and became an Apache project in 2018. It is a table format for huge analytic tables on object storage.

The KV Data Abstraction Layer, described in 2024, puts one key-value API in front of Cassandra, EVCache and other backends.

In the comparison table, Netflix's foundation is AWS; object layer S3 plus Open Connect; main online database Cassandra behind the KV layer; cache EVCache; lake Iceberg on S3; archival S3 colder classes; cloud status all AWS plus own CDN; build vs buy "buy infra, build platform".

Scale: Netflix publishes design detail more than total bytes, and the sources give no verified total for its warehouse or Cassandra fleet, so the chapter states none.

quiz.q: Why did Netflix choose Cassandra as its main online store?
quiz.a: For multi-region, always-writable replication, so any AWS region can accept writes and serve users even when another region has problems.

title: Netflix: cloud for everything except the one special thing
body: Netflix is the leading example of "cloud for everything except the one thing that is special". It buys compute and storage from AWS and runs no traditional data centers for its services. But it builds its own CDN, Open Connect, because video delivery is the core product and the bytes must sit inside ISPs close to viewers. Inside AWS, Netflix still builds a lot on top: Cassandra operations tooling, EVCache, Iceberg and, recently, a data abstraction layer.
deeper:
The logic follows the chapter's first axis: is storage your product? For Netflix, general-purpose storage and compute are not the product, so buying them from AWS lets the company focus elsewhere. Video delivery is the product, and its quality depends on bytes being physically close to viewers. No cloud region is as close as an appliance inside the viewer's ISP, so Netflix built that part.

"Buy infra, build platform" is how the comparison table summarises it. Buying infrastructure does not mean buying everything. Netflix builds substantial platform software on AWS: tooling to operate Cassandra at scale, EVCache for cross-region caching, Iceberg for analytic tables, and the KV abstraction layer.

It also separates heavy bytes from everything else. Video bytes live on Open Connect appliances and in S3, while online databases hold only metadata and user state. That keeps the databases small relative to the data volume.

The "what to steal from Netflix" list says: build only what makes your product special (the CDN), buy the rest.

quiz.q: Why does Netflix build its own CDN while buying almost all other infrastructure from AWS?
quiz.a: Video delivery is its core product and needs bytes inside ISPs near viewers; general compute and storage aren't differentiating, so buying them is better.

title: Netflix's KV layer: making future migrations cheap
body: Netflix's KV Data Abstraction Layer, described in 2024, gives application teams one stable key-value API in front of Cassandra, EVCache and other backends. Behind it, the platform team can change the storage engine, tune caching, and handle large values and pagination without every team rewriting code. Senior staff lens: this makes "move this dataset from Cassandra to something else" a platform task, not a hundred-team project. The cost is one more hop of latency and a platform team to run it.
deeper:
Without such a layer, every application team talks directly to a specific database client. Each team embeds that database's quirks: how it handles large values, how it paginates, how it retries. Moving a dataset to a different backend then requires changing every application that touches it.

With the layer, those concerns are solved once by the platform team. Large values and pagination are handled centrally. Caching can be tuned behind the API. And a backend change becomes invisible to applications.

The chapter is explicit that this is not always worth it. At Netflix's size, with many teams depending on storage, the trade is clearly worth it. At a 20-engineer startup, it is not: the latency hop and the cost of a dedicated platform team outweigh the benefit when there are few teams to migrate.

This matches the third axis: when hundreds of teams use storage, a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off choices. It is also the eighth check-your-understanding question.

quiz.q: What problem does Netflix's KV Data Abstraction Layer solve, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: One stable key-value API lets the platform change or tune backends without every team rewriting code; it costs an extra network hop and a platform team to run it.

title: How Netflix scales: active-active regions and Iceberg on S3
body: Netflix scales storage three ways. Multi-region active-active: Cassandra and EVCache replicate across AWS regions so any region can serve any user (Chapter 10). Separate the heavy bytes: video bytes live on Open Connect appliances and in S3, while online databases hold only metadata and user state. Columnar tables on S3: Iceberg was built because the older Hive table layout on object storage had slow directory listing and no safe concurrent writes (Chapter 7).
deeper:
Active-active means every region is live and serving traffic, not waiting as a standby. If one region fails, users are served by others with their data already replicated. This requires databases that accept writes in multiple regions, which is why Cassandra's always-writable replication and EVCache's cross-region replication matter.

Separating heavy bytes keeps each system doing one job. Video files are huge and immutable, so they belong on cheap object storage and on CDN appliances near viewers. Databases handle the small, frequently changing records: what a user watched, their preferences, catalog metadata. Mixing the two would make databases enormous and expensive.

Iceberg fixed two problems with Hive tables on object storage. Hive tracked a table as a set of directories, so planning a query meant listing directories, which is slow on object stores. And it had no safe way for multiple writers to change a table at once. Iceberg tracks table files in its own metadata, making listing fast and commits safe.

quiz.q: Why did Netflix build Iceberg instead of keeping Hive tables on S3?
quiz.a: Hive's directory-based layout made listing slow on object storage and gave no safe concurrent writes; Iceberg tracks files in its own metadata, fixing both.

title: Netflix migrations: seven years to AWS, and Iceberg's layout trick
body: Netflix moved from its own data centers to AWS between 2008 and 2016. The migration took about seven years, and Netflix rebuilt most of its systems as cloud-native services instead of lifting them unchanged. Its second notable migration moved Hive tables to Iceberg. Iceberg's design lets a table change its partitioning without rewriting data, which makes future layout changes a metadata operation. The sources used contain no published Netflix storage compliance design, so the chapter leaves that out.
deeper:
The AWS move shows a different migration style from Uber's. Uber lifted first (same Hadoop stack on cloud VMs) and planned to modernise later. Netflix rebuilt most systems as cloud-native services during the migration itself. That took about seven years, completing in January 2016. The advantage was ending up with systems designed for the cloud; the cost was time.

Iceberg's partition evolution is a quiet superpower. Partitioning decides how table data is grouped into files, for example by day. As data grows or query patterns change, the ideal partitioning changes too. In older layouts, changing partitioning meant rewriting the entire table, which for huge tables is costly. Iceberg records the partitioning in metadata, so new data can use a new scheme while old data stays put. Future layout changes become metadata operations.

Both migrations share a theme with the KV layer: invest in making future changes cheap. The chapter's key takeaway: abstraction layers make migrations cheap, and Netflix's KV layer and Uber's HDFS-compatible connector both hide where bytes live.

quiz.q: Why is Iceberg's ability to change partitioning without rewriting data valuable?
quiz.a: Optimal partitioning changes as data and queries evolve; Iceberg makes layout changes metadata operations instead of costly full-table rewrites.

title: LinkedIn's stack: Kafka, Espresso, Venice, Ambry and HDFS
body: LinkedIn runs its own data centers. Kafka, created at LinkedIn in 2011, is its distributed log and data movement backbone. Espresso (SIGMOD 2013) is a timeline-consistent document store on sharded MySQL with change capture. Ambry (SIGMOD 2016) is a geo-distributed object store for media, optimised for immutable blobs. Venice, in production since the end of 2016 and open-sourced in 2022, is a derived-data key-value store fed by batch pushes and streams. HDFS held over 1 EB total in 2021. Couchbase and in-process caches handle caching.
deeper:
Voldemort, from about 2009, was LinkedIn's early Dynamo-style key-value store, open source, and later replaced by Venice for read-only data.

The lake runs Spark, Trino and Iceberg, with a control plane called OpenHouse, announced in 2024.

In the comparison table, LinkedIn's foundation is HDFS; object layer Ambry; main online databases Espresso and Venice; caches Couchbase and in-process; lake HDFS plus Iceberg (OpenHouse); archival not published; own data centers; build and open-source.

Kafka is central to how the pieces connect. Espresso, the primary store, has change capture; Kafka moves data between systems; derived data is computed in Hadoop and Spark and pushed into Venice, which can also take streaming writes. That pipeline is the physical form of LinkedIn's most important idea, the separation of primary and derived data.

LinkedIn is also an unusual case in ownership: Microsoft owns it, but it keeps its own stack rather than running on Azure's storage.

quiz.q: What role does Kafka play in LinkedIn's storage stack?
quiz.a: It is the distributed log and data movement backbone, carrying changes between systems like Espresso, offline processing and Venice.

title: LinkedIn's scale: Venice pushes 1.2 PB a day
body: LinkedIn published Venice's 2022 scale: 1,800 datasets, over 300 applications, and 17 production clusters per region across 4,000 physical hosts. Venice ingests 1.2 PB and over three trillion rows per day and peaks at 45 million batch-get key lookups per second. In 2021 LinkedIn reported its Hadoop clusters together store over 1 exabyte, with the largest cluster around 10,000 nodes. These numbers show derived data is a massive workload in its own right.
deeper:
The ingestion figure is the striking one. Venice takes in 1.2 PB per day, which reflects its role: offline jobs recompute datasets like recommendations and ML features and push whole new versions. Much of what Venice stores is rebuilt regularly rather than updated in place.

The 45 million batch-get lookups per second shows the serving side: applications fetch many keys at once, for example features for many candidate items when ranking a feed.

The HDFS figure, over 1 EB with the largest cluster around 10,000 nodes, highlights the metadata challenge. A single HDFS cluster relies on one NameNode for metadata, and LinkedIn's 2021 post describes substantial work to keep that NameNode healthy at very large object counts.

In the side-by-side table, LinkedIn Venice is "4,000 hosts, 1.2 PB ingested per day" (2022) and LinkedIn HDFS "over 1 EB total" (2021). Compare with Uber's "over 1 EB in each of two regions" (2024) carefully: LinkedIn's is a total across clusters, Uber's is per region.

quiz.q: Why does Venice ingest so much data per day relative to typical databases?
quiz.a: It serves derived data that offline jobs recompute and push as whole new dataset versions, so data is regularly rebuilt rather than updated in place.

title: Primary vs derived data: LinkedIn's most important idea
body: LinkedIn's most important storage idea is separating primary data from derived data. Primary data, like a member's profile edits and messages, goes to Espresso, the source of truth. Derived data, like recommendations, "People You May Know" scores and ML features, is computed in Hadoop or Spark and pushed into Venice for fast read-only serving. Derived data can be rebuilt from primary data, so it needs less durability and can be bulk-loaded. Primary data cannot be rebuilt, so it gets careful replication and change capture.
deeper:
This split lets each store be optimised for its job. Espresso handles writes from users and must never lose them, so it emphasises replication and change capture, which also feeds downstream processing. Venice handles enormous read volumes of data that can always be recomputed, so it can accept bulk loads and simpler durability.

The consequences are practical. If Venice lost a dataset, LinkedIn could recompute it from primary data and push it again. If Espresso lost a message, it would be gone. Spending equal durability effort on both would waste money on derived data or under-protect primary data.

Bulk loading also suits how derived data is produced: an offline job computes a whole new version at once, so swapping in the new version is more efficient than applying millions of individual updates.

This is the chapter's fourth check-your-understanding question. The "what to steal from LinkedIn" list sums it up: derived data is rebuilt, bulk-pushed and version-swapped; primary data is guarded.

quiz.q: What is the difference between primary and derived data at LinkedIn, and how does it change storage choices?
quiz.a: Primary data is the source of truth and cannot be rebuilt, so Espresso replicates it carefully. Derived data is recomputable, so Venice bulk-loads and version-swaps it with lower durability needs.

title: In industry: LinkedIn paused its move to Azure
body: In industry: in 2019 LinkedIn announced a plan to move its data centers to Azure, the cloud of its owner, Microsoft. In 2022 it paused that plan and kept its own data centers, citing the value of its existing on-prem investment. It is a public example of a large company deciding that a full cloud move was not worth it at that time. Even common ownership with a cloud provider did not make migration automatically worthwhile.
deeper:
This case is a useful counterweight to the assumption that every company eventually moves fully to public cloud. Netflix did, over about seven years. Uber is moving its data lake to Google Cloud and partnering with Oracle Cloud. But LinkedIn weighed the cost of moving against what it already had and decided to stay on-prem, at least for then.

What does "value of existing on-prem investment" mean in storage terms? LinkedIn had built and tuned an extensive stack: HDFS storing over 1 exabyte, Venice across 4,000 hosts, Espresso, Ambry and Kafka. Migrating all of that is expensive and risky, and the benefits must outweigh both the migration cost and any ongoing price difference.

It also fits Microsoft's broader philosophy noted in the chapter: Microsoft buys companies like LinkedIn and GitHub, which keep their own stacks, rather than forcing them onto Azure.

The lesson for senior engineers: cloud vs on-prem is a cost-structure and timing decision, not a one-way trend. Re-evaluating a planned migration is legitimate.

quiz.q: What does LinkedIn's 2022 decision about Azure illustrate?
quiz.a: A large company can reasonably decide a full cloud move is not worth it at a given time, weighing migration cost against existing on-prem investment, even with a cloud-owning parent.

title: Venice's atomic version swaps and LinkedIn's NameNode struggle
body: LinkedIn scales serving with push-based Venice. Offline jobs push whole new versions of a dataset, and Venice swaps versions atomically, so reads never see a half-loaded dataset. On the analytics side, LinkedIn scales HDFS both vertically and horizontally. Its 2021 post describes a lot of work to keep a single NameNode, the HDFS metadata server, healthy at very large object counts. That is the HDFS metadata bottleneck from Chapter 2 in real life.
deeper:
Atomic version swaps solve a consistency problem specific to bulk loads. If a new version of, say, recommendation scores were loaded key by key into the live dataset, readers during the load would see a mix of old and new values, possibly inconsistent with each other. Venice instead loads the new version alongside the old one and switches reads over in one step once it is complete.

The NameNode story contrasts with Google and Meta. HDFS keeps all file system metadata in a single NameNode's memory, just as GFS's master did. As object counts grow, that one server's memory and performance become the limit. Google replaced its equivalent with Colossus on Bigtable; Meta replaced HDFS with Tectonic's metadata in ZippyDB. LinkedIn instead invested in keeping the NameNode healthy while its clusters grew past 1 exabyte in total, with the largest around 10,000 nodes.

Both show the same lesson from different angles: metadata is usually what breaks first.

quiz.q: Why does Venice swap dataset versions atomically instead of updating keys in place during a push?
quiz.a: So reads never see a half-loaded mix of old and new values; the complete new version replaces the old in one step.

title: LinkedIn's migrations: Voldemort to Venice, Hive to Iceberg
body: LinkedIn's notable storage migrations: Voldemort to Venice, where the read-only Voldemort use case was replaced by Venice, which added streaming (hybrid) writes on top of batch pushes. And Hive to Iceberg, where LinkedIn moved its lake toward Iceberg tables with a control plane called OpenHouse, announced in 2024, so table policies like retention are managed centrally. On compliance, LinkedIn applies GDPR controls and has presented data deletion work, but no detailed design is described.
deeper:
Voldemort was an early Dynamo-style key-value store from about 2009, used for serving read-only data produced offline. Venice kept that batch-push model but added hybrid writes: streaming updates layered on top of batch pushes. That means a dataset can be rebuilt in bulk periodically while also receiving fresh updates between rebuilds, so served data stays more current.

OpenHouse addresses a governance problem in lakes. When thousands of tables are managed by different teams, policies like how long to keep data are applied inconsistently. A central control plane lets the platform enforce retention and similar rules across tables. That connects to compliance: retention and deletion are central to regulations like GDPR.

On compliance itself, the chapter applies its accuracy rule. LinkedIn applies GDPR controls across its data platform and has presented work on data deletion and purging at conferences, but the sources used do not give a detailed design, so the chapter does not describe one.

Iceberg adoption links LinkedIn with Netflix, where Iceberg was created.

quiz.q: What did Venice add over the Voldemort read-only use case it replaced?
quiz.a: Streaming (hybrid) writes on top of batch pushes, so datasets can receive fresh updates between bulk rebuilds.

title: Magic Pocket: Dropbox's own block storage
body: Magic Pocket, made public in 2016, is Dropbox's own block storage for file contents. Files are split into blocks of up to 4 MB, each identified by its SHA-256 hash. Blocks are grouped into 1 GB buckets. Storage is organised into cells of about 50 PB raw. A sharded MySQL Block Index maps block hashes to locations. Repair starts after a storage node has been offline for 15 minutes. Dropbox's philosophy for it: "keep it simple".
deeper:
Identifying blocks by SHA-256 hash is content addressing: the name of a block is derived from its contents. Identical blocks get identical names, and blocks never change, since a changed block would be a different hash. That immutability is what makes the rest of the design simple.

Grouping blocks into 1 GB buckets reduces the number of units the system tracks and moves, much as Haystack packed many photos into large files.

The Block Index in sharded MySQL is the metadata: given a hash, where does the block live? Using MySQL again reflects building on proven engines.

The 15-minute repair delay is a trade-off. Starting repair instantly would waste bandwidth rebuilding data for nodes that come back after a brief reboot. Waiting too long risks further failures before redundancy is restored.

"Keep it simple" shows in the architecture: a central master per cell, no distributed consensus in the data path, and a very small team. The side-by-side table lists Magic Pocket as "cells about 50 PB raw, multi-EB total" (2016).

quiz.q: Why does identifying blocks by SHA-256 hash simplify Magic Pocket's design?
quiz.a: Blocks become content-addressed and immutable: a block's name derives from its contents and never changes, which removes update and consistency complexity.

title: Dropbox's S3 exit: dark launch, then gradual cutover
body: Dropbox moved its user data off Amazon S3 onto Magic Pocket. It dark-launched the new system in August 2014, stored new files only in-house from February 2015, and had moved over 90 percent of user data off S3 by October 2015. The reasons: end-to-end control of performance, and better unit economics at Dropbox's scale. Dropbox still uses AWS where it makes sense, especially outside the US.
deeper:
A dark launch means running the new system with real traffic in the background without depending on it for users yet. Dropbox mirrored data into Magic Pocket for months, proving it could store and serve correctly before any user relied on it. The "what to steal from Dropbox" list recommends exactly this: dark-launch a new store by mirroring for months before cutting over.

The cutover was staged: first new files went only in-house (February 2015), then existing data migrated until over 90 percent was moved (October 2015). At each stage, S3 still held data, so the move was gradual and reversible. The key takeaways group it with Meta's MyRocks and Uber's GCP moves as migrations using dual running and gradual cutover.

The reasons connect to the chapter's axes. Dropbox's product is file storage, and storage is a large share of its costs, so owning the stack pays.

The chapter's third check-your-understanding question adds the caveat: most companies should not copy this, because storage is not their main cost and they lack the scale to amortise a storage team.

quiz.q: Give two reasons Dropbox moved off S3, and one reason most companies should not copy it.
quiz.a: Full-stack performance control and better unit economics at its scale. Most companies shouldn't copy it: storage isn't their main cost and they lack scale to amortise a storage team.

title: Senior staff lens: when buy-then-build pays off
body: Senior staff lens: Dropbox is the classic case where buy then build paid off. When storage is most of your cost and your workload is simple, like immutable blocks, owning the stack pays. When storage is a small part of your cost, it rarely does. Dropbox's "keep it simple" philosophy made building feasible: a central master per cell, no distributed consensus in the data path, and a very small team running exabyte-scale storage.
deeper:
Two conditions made building work for Dropbox, and both matter.

First, cost structure. Dropbox stores users' files; storage is both its product and a dominant cost. Improving unit economics on storage directly improves the business. For a company where storage is a minor line item, even a large percentage saving is a small absolute amount, and it will not pay for a dedicated storage engineering team.

Second, workload simplicity. Magic Pocket stores immutable, content-addressed blocks. There are no in-place updates, no complex queries and no cross-object transactions. That let Dropbox avoid distributed consensus in the data path and run with a central master per cell. A more complex workload would demand a much bigger and more experienced team.

Buying first also mattered. Starting on S3 let Dropbox grow without building storage too early, and it moved only once its scale justified the investment.

The "what to steal from Dropbox" list: "keep it simple" works at exabyte scale when the data model is simple.

quiz.q: What two conditions made building its own storage pay off for Dropbox?
quiz.a: Storage was most of its cost (and its product), and its workload was simple: immutable, content-addressed blocks, allowing a small team and no consensus in the data path.

title: Apple: billions of tiny databases on FoundationDB
body: Apple publishes little about its infrastructure, but FoundationDB is public. Apple acquired FoundationDB in 2015 and open-sourced it in 2018. The 2019 Record Layer paper says CloudKit uses the Record Layer on FoundationDB to host billions of independent logical databases, one per user per app, serving hundreds of millions of users. Each tiny database is a key-prefix range inside a shared FoundationDB cluster. This is multi-tenancy at the extreme.
deeper:
FoundationDB is a strongly consistent, ordered, transactional key-value store. "Ordered" means keys are sorted, so all keys sharing a prefix sit together. Apple exploits that: each user-app database is simply a range of keys with a common prefix. Creating a new database costs almost nothing; it is just a new prefix, not a new server or cluster.

The Record Layer is a stateless layer on top of FoundationDB that adds records, indexes and queries. Because it is stateless, it scales by adding instances, while FoundationDB provides durability and transactions. Indexes can be maintained transactionally together with records, which avoids the index-data disagreements Pinterest hit.

The chapter draws the general pattern: a single strongly consistent, ordered key-value core with thin stateless layers on top.

In the comparison table, Apple's main online database is FoundationDB plus Record Layer; its DFS, object, cache, lake and archival layers are not published; cloud vs on-prem is "mixed, not detailed"; build vs buy is "acquired and built". The "what to steal" list: such a core can host billions of tiny tenant databases.

quiz.q: How can FoundationDB host billions of separate CloudKit databases?
quiz.a: Each database is a key-prefix range in a shared ordered key-value cluster, so a new database is just a new prefix; the stateless Record Layer adds records, indexes and queries.

title: Apple's Advanced Data Protection: Apple holds no keys
body: Advanced Data Protection, launched by Apple in 2022, lets users turn on end-to-end encryption for most iCloud data categories. With it enabled, Apple does not hold the keys, so it cannot decrypt that data on its servers. It is one of only two storage facts Apple has made public in this chapter, alongside FoundationDB. Like Meta's default Messenger encryption, it changes what the server can do with stored data.
deeper:
The distinction from ordinary encryption at rest is who holds the keys. The big clouds encrypt data at rest by default (AWS S3 since 2023, Azure Storage, Google Cloud), but the provider manages or can access keys, so servers can still process the data. End-to-end encryption leaves keys only on users' devices.

For storage systems, that means the server holds ciphertext for those categories. Server-side features that need to read content cannot work on that data; they must run on devices, if at all.

Note two details. First, ADP is opt-in: users turn it on, unlike Meta's Messenger, where end-to-end encryption became the default in December 2023. Second, it covers most iCloud data categories, not necessarily all.

The chapter's key takeaways pair them: end-to-end encryption (Meta Messenger, Apple ADP) changes what the server can do with stored data. For architects, it is a design constraint to settle early, because retrofitting it removes server-side capabilities that products may depend on.

quiz.q: How does Apple's ADP differ from the default encryption at rest offered by big clouds?
quiz.a: With ADP, keys stay with users so Apple cannot decrypt the data; with encryption at rest, the provider manages keys and servers can still process the data.

title: Pinterest moved its graph from HBase to TiDB
body: Pinterest runs on AWS and historically used HBase heavily for online storage. Its graph service, Zen, was built on HBase and MySQL in 2014. Pinterest later moved this to TiDB, a distributed SQL database, as PinGraph. The published case study reports 1.5 PB of data, 8 million queries per second at peak, over 100 use cases, up to 10x lower P99 latency and over 50 percent lower infrastructure cost.
deeper:
The case study gives three reasons for the move: data inconsistencies caused by application-level secondary indexes, limited query patterns, and a 10-year-old codebase.

The first reason is the most instructive. HBase did not give Zen transactions across the data and its secondary indexes, so the application maintained indexes itself, and failures could leave them out of sync. A distributed SQL database with native transactions and indexes removes that class of bugs.

Limited query patterns follow from building on a key-value style store: every new way of querying needed application code. SQL offers more flexible queries out of the box.

The results are notable: up to 10x lower P99 latency (the latency 99 percent of requests beat) and over 50 percent lower infrastructure cost at 1.5 PB and 8 million QPS peak.

In the comparison table, Pinterest's foundation is AWS; object store S3; online database TiDB, formerly HBase; cloud status AWS; build vs buy "buy infra, adopt open source". The side-by-side table lists PinGraph as "1.5 PB, 8M QPS peak" (case study, 2020s).

quiz.q: What reasons did Pinterest give for moving its graph service from HBase to TiDB?
quiz.a: Data inconsistencies from application-level secondary indexes, limited query patterns, and a 10-year-old codebase.

title: Common mistake: app-built secondary indexes without transactions
body: Common mistake: building secondary indexes in application code on top of a store that has no transactions. The application writes the data, then writes the index entry, as two separate operations. It works until a failure happens between the two writes. Then the index and the data disagree forever: queries by the index miss records or point to wrong ones. Pinterest named this as a main reason to migrate its graph service from HBase to TiDB.
deeper:
Why "forever"? Nothing in the system notices the mismatch. The store has no transaction to roll back the half-finished pair of writes, and nothing later repairs it unless someone builds a reconciliation job. Over years and many failures, inconsistencies accumulate.

The fix is to let the database maintain indexes transactionally, so the data write and index write commit together or not at all. Pinterest's move to TiDB, a distributed SQL database with native transactions, removed this class of bugs. The "what to steal from Pinterest" list says: do not build secondary indexes in application code without transactions.

Other systems in the chapter take the safe path. Apple's FoundationDB Record Layer adds indexes on top of a transactional key-value core. Uber's Docstore provides materialized views and change data capture so teams can read by a second key without building their own pipelines.

If you must index in application code, you need either transactions or a background process that detects and repairs mismatches, and you should expect to pay for that complexity.

quiz.q: Why do application-maintained secondary indexes on a non-transactional store eventually go wrong?
quiz.a: Data and index are separate writes; a failure between them leaves them disagreeing, and nothing rolls back or repairs the mismatch, so errors accumulate.

title: The comparison table: everyone has a foundation layer
body: Lined up side by side, each company's foundation layer is clear. Google: Colossus. AWS: ShardStore storage nodes and EBS. Meta: Tectonic. Microsoft: the stream layer inside stamps. Uber: HDFS, moving to Google Cloud Storage. Netflix and Pinterest: AWS. LinkedIn: HDFS. Dropbox: Magic Pocket. Apple: not published. The object layers are GCS, S3, Tectonic's blob tenant, Azure Blob and ADLS Gen2, HDFS or cloud object storage, S3 plus Open Connect, Ambry, Magic Pocket and S3 again.
deeper:
The database and cache columns show more variety. Online databases: Bigtable and Spanner (Google); DynamoDB and Aurora (AWS); MySQL/MyRocks and ZippyDB (Meta); Cosmos DB and Azure SQL (Microsoft); Docstore on MySQL and Cassandra (Uber); Cassandra behind a KV layer (Netflix); Espresso and Venice (LinkedIn); MySQL Edgestore (Dropbox); FoundationDB plus Record Layer (Apple); TiDB, formerly HBase (Pinterest).

Caches: in-process and Memorystore at Google; ElastiCache and MemoryDB at AWS; Memcache and TAO at Meta; Azure Cache for Redis; Redis CacheFront at Uber; EVCache at Netflix; Couchbase and in-process at LinkedIn.

Lakes: BigQuery (Dremel, Capacitor); S3 plus Athena, Redshift, S3 Tables; Tectonic plus Presto/Spark; ADLS plus Synapse/Fabric; Hudi, Hive, Presto; Iceberg on S3; HDFS plus Iceberg with OpenHouse.

Archival: colder media and Archive class; Glacier classes; cold storage tiers; Archive tier and Silica research; cheaper tiers; S3 colder classes; Magic Pocket cold tier. Several cells say "not published" or "not covered".

MySQL appears again and again: Meta, Uber, LinkedIn, Dropbox and Pinterest's old Zen.

quiz.q: What pattern does the comparison table reveal about the lowest layer across companies?
quiz.a: Nearly every company has one foundation layer (Colossus, Tectonic, stream layer, ShardStore, Magic Pocket, HDFS or AWS itself) under many different databases, caches and lakes.

title: Cloud vs on-prem and build vs buy, company by company
body: The comparison table's last two columns summarise strategy. Google: own data centers, builds almost everything. AWS: is the cloud, builds, and retail uses AWS. Meta: own data centers, builds and open-sources. Microsoft: is the cloud, builds core, buys companies. Uber: moving to Oracle Cloud and Google Cloud, thin layers on open source. Netflix: all AWS plus own CDN, buys infrastructure and builds platform. LinkedIn: own data centers, builds and open-sources. Dropbox: own plus some AWS, moved from buy to build. Apple: mixed, acquired and built. Pinterest: AWS, buys infrastructure and adopts open source.
deeper:
Read these columns together and groups appear.

The pure builders run their own data centers: Google, Meta, LinkedIn. They have scale, many internal teams and a history of publishing and open-sourcing their systems.

The clouds, AWS and Microsoft, build because storage is what they sell.

The cloud buyers, Netflix and Pinterest, rent infrastructure and invest their engineering higher up: Netflix in platform software and its CDN, Pinterest in adopting open source like TiDB.

The movers are the most interesting. Dropbox went from buying (S3) to building (Magic Pocket) because storage was its product and main cost. Uber went the other direction, from its own data centers toward public cloud. LinkedIn planned to move to Azure and then paused.

Apple is the outlier: mixed and not detailed, acquiring FoundationDB and building on it.

No single strategy wins. The chapter's three axes, whether storage is your product, how big your storage bill is, and how many teams you serve, explain why each company landed where it did.

quiz.q: Dropbox and Uber moved in opposite directions on cloud vs own infrastructure. What explains the difference?
quiz.a: Storage is Dropbox's product and main cost, so owning it pays; for Uber storage isn't the product, so moving the lake to public cloud made more sense.

title: Comparing published scale numbers without fooling yourself
body: The chapter lines up published scale numbers with years. AWS S3: 700+ trillion objects, 200M+ requests per second average, hundreds of EB (2026). DynamoDB: 146M requests per second peak (2024). EBS: 264 PB provisioned for Prime Day (2024). Meta Tectonic: 1,590 PB in one cluster (2021). Haystack: 260 billion images, 20 PB (2010). f4: 65 PB warm (2014). TAO: about 1 billion reads per second (2013). Colossus: exabyte clusters, 100x GFS metadata (2021). Rapid Storage: 20M requests per second per bucket (2025).
deeper:
The rest of the table: Azure WAS 70 PB raw, stamps up to 30 PB (2011); Uber Hadoop over 1 EB in each of two regions (2024); Uber Docstore tens of PB, tens of millions of QPS (2020); LinkedIn Venice 4,000 hosts, 1.2 PB ingested per day (2022); LinkedIn HDFS over 1 EB total (2021); Dropbox Magic Pocket cells about 50 PB raw, multi-EB total (2016); Pinterest PinGraph on TiDB 1.5 PB, 8M QPS peak (case study, 2020s).

The chapter's key takeaway: published numbers differ in kind and year. Always compare with the year and the unit in mind.

The table mixes several kinds of figure. Some are capacity (PB, EB), some are object counts, some are request rates, and request rates can be averages or peaks, per second or per minute. Scope varies too: one cluster (Tectonic), one bucket (Rapid Storage), one region (Uber), a whole fleet (S3), one event (Prime Day). Years range from 2010 to 2026, a span in which storage grew enormously.

Saying "Azure is smaller than Meta" from 70 PB (2011) versus 1,590 PB (2021) would be meaningless on both counts.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to compare Azure's 70 PB (2011) with Meta Tectonic's 1,590 PB (2021)?
quiz.a: They differ in year by a decade and in scope (Azure fleet raw storage vs one Tectonic cluster's capacity), so the comparison says nothing about current relative size.

section: Three axes that explain the differences
title: Axis 1: is storage your product?
body: The first axis explaining company differences: is storage your product? AWS, Azure and Google Cloud sell storage, so they must build it. Dropbox's product is file storage, so it rebuilt its storage in-house rather than keep renting S3. Netflix's product is video, so it built the part that serves video, the Open Connect CDN, and bought the rest from AWS. The closer storage is to what customers pay for, the stronger the case for building it.
deeper:
The axis turns a vague build-vs-buy debate into a sharp question: would owning this layer make your product better in a way customers notice?

For the clouds, the answer is trivially yes; storage services are the product line. For Dropbox, control over storage performance and cost directly shapes the product it sells. For Netflix, general-purpose storage makes no visible difference to viewers, but video delivery quality does, so it builds only that.

The axis also cautions against copying giants blindly. A product company reading about Colossus or Tectonic might be tempted to build its own distributed file system. Unless storage is its product, the effort goes into something customers do not value.

The chapter's key takeaway phrases the combined rule: build vs buy follows your cost structure. If storage is your product or your largest cost, building pays. Otherwise, buy and build only thin layers, as Uber does on MySQL and HDFS, and as Netflix does with its platform software on AWS.

quiz.q: Why did Netflix build Open Connect but not its own general-purpose storage, according to the first axis?
quiz.a: Video delivery is Netflix's product, so owning the CDN improves what customers pay for; general storage doesn't differentiate, so it buys that from AWS.

section: Three axes that explain the differences
title: Axis 2: how big is your storage bill?
body: The second axis: how large is your storage bill as a share of total cost? When storage dominates cost, as at Dropbox and in Meta's photo storage, owning the hardware and the erasure codes pays for a dedicated team. When it does not, as at most product companies, buying wins. The logic is amortisation: a storage engineering team is a large fixed cost, and only a big enough storage bill makes the savings exceed it.
deeper:
Consider what owning storage lets you optimise. You choose hardware and pack it efficiently. You pick erasure codes that cut overhead, like f4's effective replication factor of 2.1 instead of 3.6, or Azure's LRC reducing overhead compared with triple replication. You consolidate fleets to stop stranding IOPS or capacity, as Tectonic did. At Azure's size, the chapter notes, a small cut in overhead is a very large saving.

Each of those savings is a percentage of the storage bill. If the bill is huge, a few percent pays for a whole team. If the bill is small, the same percentage does not cover one engineer.

This is why the chapter's answer to "should most companies copy Dropbox's S3 exit?" is no: storage is not their main cost and they lack the scale to amortise a storage team.

The axis also explains why Meta built so heavily for photos: over 260 billion images in 2010 and 65 PB of warm blobs in 2014 made storage efficiency a major cost lever.

quiz.q: Why does the size of the storage bill determine whether building your own storage pays off?
quiz.a: Storage teams are a large fixed cost; efficiency gains are a percentage of the bill, so only a big bill yields savings exceeding the team's cost.

section: Three axes that explain the differences
title: Axis 3: how many teams must you serve?
body: The third axis: how many teams must your storage serve? When hundreds of teams use storage, as at Meta, Google and Netflix, a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off choices. When only a handful of teams do, polyglot by team, where each team picks its own database, is fine. The number of consumers decides whether standardisation and platform investment are worth their cost.
deeper:
With many teams, one-off choices multiply: dozens of databases, each with its own operations, upgrades, failure modes and migration pain. A shared foundation concentrates expertise and lets improvements reach everyone. An abstraction layer, like Netflix's KV layer, means backend changes do not ripple into hundreds of codebases.

With few teams, those benefits shrink while the costs stay. A platform team, an extra network hop and the effort of building shared layers are overhead a small organisation cannot justify. The chapter makes this concrete in the Netflix senior staff lens: the KV layer is clearly worth it at Netflix's size, but not at a 20-engineer startup.

This axis connects to AWS's polyglot philosophy too. AWS sells many purpose-built databases and tells customers to pick the right tool for the job. For a small customer, polyglot is fine. For a large organisation adopting many AWS databases across hundreds of teams, the third axis suggests adding a shared layer or standard on top.

quiz.q: Why is polyglot-by-team storage acceptable for a small company but costly for a large one?
quiz.a: With few teams, platform overhead outweighs benefits; with hundreds, divergent databases multiply operations and migration pain, so a shared foundation plus abstraction layer wins.

title: What to steal from Google, AWS and Meta
body: From Google: store your metadata in a sharded database you already trust, let a single distributed file system serve every higher layer, and tier by temperature inside the storage system so users do not have to. From AWS: choose one primary goal for a shared service, as DynamoDB chose predictable latency; upgrade guarantees in place without API changes, as S3 did with strong consistency; and use formal methods and reference models for storage node code. From Meta: watch for stranded resources.
deeper:
Meta's full list: if one fleet is IOPS-bound and another is capacity-bound, consolidate them. Let each tenant pick its encoding, using replicate-then-re-encode for small appends and Reed-Solomon for sealed data. Migrate engines with dual replication and checksums so you can always roll back, as with MyRocks.

What ties these together is that each lesson is about making a large shared storage system efficient and safe to change.

Google's lessons are about structure: metadata scaling via a trusted sharded store, one foundation, automatic tiering.

AWS's lessons are about discipline in design and change: a single written primary goal keeps trade-offs consistent; in-place contract upgrades avoid forcing customers to migrate; formal methods let engineers change storage code at exabyte scale without corrupting data.

Meta's lessons are about efficiency and safe migration: detect stranded IOPS or capacity, tailor durability per tenant within one file system, and keep every migration reversible.

You do not need Google's or Meta's scale to use most of these. Writing down one primary goal, or migrating with dual replication and checksums, applies at any size.

quiz.q: Which lesson from Meta applies when one fleet runs out of IOPS while another runs out of disk space?
quiz.a: Consolidate them onto shared storage so IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants balance each other, as Tectonic did for Haystack and f4.

title: What to steal from Azure, Uber, Netflix and LinkedIn
body: From Azure: make the unit of growth a fixed-size stamp, keep it below a utilization ceiling, move accounts between stamps, and invest in erasure codes, since small overhead cuts are large savings at scale. From Uber: change one thing at a time in a migration, move bytes behind a compatible API first, federate access through proxies, modernize engines later, and build thin layers on proven engines like MySQL. From Netflix: put a data abstraction layer between applications and databases. From LinkedIn: separate primary data from derived data.
deeper:
Netflix's full lesson: the abstraction layer lets you change backends without touching every team, and you should build only what makes your product special (the CDN) and buy the rest. LinkedIn's full lesson: derived data is rebuilt, bulk-pushed and version-swapped; primary data is guarded.

These lessons lean toward operations and evolution.

Azure's stamps make growth predictable and failures contained. The utilization ceiling (around 70 percent in the WAS paper) keeps headroom, and account moves handle rebalancing. Erasure code investment like LRC turns engineering effort into large hardware savings.

Uber's lessons are a migration playbook: separate storage moves from engine moves, hide location behind compatible APIs and proxies, replicate both directions during transition, then modernise. Its thin-layer approach keeps risky storage engine work in proven code.

Netflix's abstraction layer is an investment in cheap future migrations, sensible when many teams depend on storage.

LinkedIn's primary vs derived split tells you where to spend durability effort: guard what cannot be rebuilt; bulk-load and version-swap what can.

quiz.q: According to Uber's lesson, in what order should an exabyte-scale migration change things?
quiz.a: Move bytes first behind a compatible API, federate access through proxies, and only then modernize compute engines, changing one thing at a time.

title: What to steal from Dropbox, Apple and Pinterest
body: From Dropbox: "keep it simple" works at exabyte scale when the data model is simple, meaning immutable, content-addressed blocks; and dark-launch a new store by mirroring for months before cutting over. From Apple: a single ordered, transactional key-value core with stateless layers above can host billions of tiny tenant databases. From Pinterest: do not build secondary indexes in application code without transactions; moving to a database with native transactions removed a class of bugs.
deeper:
The Dropbox lesson has a precondition. Simplicity (a central master per cell, no distributed consensus in the data path, a very small team) was only possible because blocks never change. If your data model involves in-place updates and complex queries, the same minimalism will not hold. The dark-launch lesson is universal: mirror real traffic into a new store for months, as Dropbox did from August 2014, before users depend on it.

Apple's lesson is about multi-tenancy. Rather than a database server per tenant, make each tenant a key-prefix range in a shared, ordered, transactional store, and put stateless logic (records, indexes, queries) in a layer above. Adding a tenant costs almost nothing, and the stateless layer scales by adding instances. CloudKit uses this for billions of per-user, per-app databases.

Pinterest's lesson is a warning. Two separate writes for data and index, without a transaction, will eventually disagree after a failure, and nothing repairs it. Let the database maintain indexes atomically.

Notice how these echo each other: Apple's transactional core with indexes is exactly what Pinterest lacked on HBase.

quiz.q: What precondition made Dropbox's 'keep it simple' design work at exabyte scale?
quiz.a: A simple data model: immutable, content-addressed blocks, which removed the need for distributed consensus in the data path.

title: Takeaways: foundations, metadata, consolidation, cost
body: Four of the chapter's key takeaways. Most giants build one shared storage foundation, such as Colossus, Tectonic, Azure's stream layer or S3's storage nodes, and many specialised systems on top. Metadata scaling drove the biggest redesigns, GFS to Colossus and HDFS to Tectonic, and both moved metadata into a sharded key-value store. Specialize, then consolidate is a common arc; stranded IOPS and stranded capacity signal it is time. Build vs buy follows cost structure: if storage is your product or largest cost, building pays.
deeper:
The build-vs-buy takeaway continues: otherwise, buy and build only thin layers.

These four fit together as a model of how large storage organisations evolve. Early on, teams build or adopt specialised systems per workload and learn them. As scale grows, two pressures appear. First, metadata: single-master designs like GFS and HDFS hit memory and performance limits, and the fix is to put metadata in a sharded store you already trust (Bigtable for Colossus, ZippyDB for Tectonic). Second, efficiency: separate fleets strand different resources, like Haystack's idle capacity and f4's idle IOPS, and consolidation onto one foundation recovers them.

The end state is the recurring pattern: one foundation where scale and cost live, many specialised systems where product needs live.

Whether a company should walk this path itself depends on cost structure. Google, Meta, AWS, Azure and Dropbox have storage as their product or a dominant cost. Netflix, Pinterest and increasingly Uber buy infrastructure and build thin layers or platform software on top.

quiz.q: According to the key takeaways, what drove the biggest storage redesigns in this chapter?
quiz.a: Metadata scaling: GFS to Colossus and HDFS to Tectonic, both moving metadata from a single master into a sharded key-value store.

title: Takeaways: abstractions, reversible migrations, encryption, numbers
body: Four more key takeaways. Abstraction layers make migrations cheap: Netflix's KV layer and Uber's HDFS-compatible cloud connector both hide where bytes live. Good migrations are reversible and change one thing at a time: Meta's MyRocks move, Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit all used dual running and gradual cutover. Encryption at rest is now a default, not an option, at AWS S3 (2023), Azure Storage and Google Cloud. Published numbers differ in kind and year, so always compare with the year and unit in mind.
deeper:
The encryption takeaway has a second half: end-to-end encryption, as in Meta Messenger (default since December 2023) and Apple's Advanced Data Protection (2022), changes what the server can do with stored data, because the server no longer holds keys and cannot search or index content.

The first two takeaways are the practical heart of the chapter for anyone who operates storage. Systems will change: engines get replaced, data moves to new infrastructure, guarantees get upgraded. What separates smooth changes from painful ones is preparation. A stable interface in front of storage, whether a client library (Google), an unchanged API (S3), a KV abstraction (Netflix) or a compatible connector (Uber), lets the backend change without touching every user. Dual running, with replication both ways, checksums and shadow traffic, keeps every step reversible.

The numbers takeaway is a habit of mind. Figures in this chapter range from 2010 to 2026 and mix capacity, object counts, averages, peaks and per-cluster or per-bucket scopes. Before comparing, check the year, the unit and the scope.

quiz.q: What do Meta's MyRocks move, Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit have in common?
quiz.a: All used dual running and gradual cutover, keeping each step reversible and changing one thing at a time.
